title: Drafting, editing and critique are three different asks
description: “Make this better” collapses three genuinely different jobs — write it, fix it, or just tell me what's wrong with it — and the model resolves the ambiguity itself unless you don't let it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish drafting, editing and critique as three different tasks with different failure modes
Word a request so it produces the specific one of the three you actually wanted

contentSections.title: One instruction, three different jobs

contentSections.body: A freelancer pastes her own rough pitch email into an AI tool and types “make this better.” What comes back is fluent and polished — and isn't her pitch anymore. Different opening, different structure, half her original points gone. She wanted three sentences tightened. She got a stranger's email wearing her subject line.

contentSections.question: Before the mechanism: when you paste a full draft and type “make this better,” does the model default to improving what's there, or to writing the real version from scratch?
contentSections.answer: There's no reliable default — “make this better” is genuinely ambiguous between edit and rewrite, and the model resolves that ambiguity itself, often toward the more thorough-looking option, because a fuller rewrite reads as more helpful than three small tracked changes.
contentSections.hint: Which output looks more impressive to produce: three specific line edits, or an entirely new paragraph?

contentSections.body:
“Help me write this” is actually three different jobs, and they fail differently. **Drafting** starts from nothing, or from bullet points — you want full text produced. **Editing** starts from your actual existing sentences, and you want only the specific problems fixed (grammar, clarity, a clunky transition) with everything else left alone. **Critique** wants no rewriting at all — just an honest read on what's working and what isn't, with the writing itself untouched.

Each has its own realistic way of going wrong. Drafting risks something fluent but generic — correct, readable, and in nobody's specific voice. Editing risks the model quietly rewriting far more than you asked, discarding your actual sentences instead of repairing them. Critique risks being too polite and vague to tell you anything you can act on — that one gets its own lesson later in this module. Naming which of the three you want, out loud, in the prompt, is most of the fix for all three.

contentSections.code:
Prompt (with a full paragraph pasted in): “Improve this.”
Output: a completely different paragraph — same topic, new structure, none of the original sentences kept.
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw here — in the prompt, not in the AI?

options.label: “Improve this” never specifies whether “this” means edit-in-place or replace entirely — the ambiguity is in the request, and the model picked the reading that produces the more impressive-looking output
The AI is simply bad at editing and can only rewrite from scratch
You should always ask for a full rewrite anyway, since it's more thorough

feedback.ambiguous: Right — the model can absolutely make small, targeted edits when asked to. The prompt never asked for that; it left the scope open, and the model filled the gap with the reading that looks most like effort.
feedback.cant-edit: Models edit in place fine when told to — “change only X, keep the rest as written” works. The failure here is the missing instruction, not a missing capability.
feedback.always-rewrite: That throws away the actual point of editing — keeping your own sentences and fixing only what's broken. A full rewrite is sometimes right, but only when that's genuinely what you wanted.

contentSections.flawExplanation: “Improve this” names a goal (better) but not a method (how much may change). Without that boundary, the model has no way to know a light edit was wanted instead of a rewrite — and it isn't going to guess conservatively by default.

contentSections.body: Say which of the three jobs you want — draft, edit, or critique — because “make this better” doesn't specify, and the model will pick for you.

contentSections.title: Naming which one you want

contentSections.body: A support-group organizer wants a read on a post before she publishes it — not a rewrite, just “is this going to land wrong with anyone.” She types “what do you think of this?” and gets back a fully rewritten version she never asked for, on top of no real feedback.

contentSections.scenario: The same organizer tries again later with a different post: “Don't rewrite anything. Just tell me what's working and what isn't.” This time she gets actual, untouched-text feedback.
contentSections.question: Why would the same model behave so differently to two similar-sounding requests?

options.label: A vague request (“what do you think”) leaves the model to default toward the most “helpful-looking” output, which is usually a rewrite — an explicit “don't rewrite, just tell me” removes that default
The model can't produce feedback without rewriting unless specifically forbidden to
The second post was better written, so there was less to change

feedback.default: That's the actual lever — removing the ambiguity, not the post's quality or the model's raw ability, is what changed the output. “Don't rewrite” closes off the reading that produced an unwanted rewrite the first time.
feedback.cant-feedback: The model can absolutely give feedback without touching the text — lesson 3 covers this directly. The issue the first time was that nothing ruled a rewrite out.
feedback.quality: Nothing about the post's quality changed what “what do you think” leaves open — the fix was in what was asked for, not in what was pasted in.

contentSections.mechanism: An instruction that only states the goal (better feedback, a better draft) leaves the model to choose the method. Naming the method — draft / edit-in-place / feedback-only, no rewrite — removes that choice from the model.

contentSections.body: In practice, that means being explicit about the method, not just the goal. For a draft: “Draft a first version of X from these bullet points.” For an edit: “Edit this paragraph — fix only clarity and grammar, keep my structure and my wording as close to the original as you can.” For a critique: “Don't rewrite anything. Just tell me what's working and what isn't, and be specific.” None of these are longer or more effortful to type than “make this better” — they just remove the one piece of information the model was missing.
“Make this better” names a goal, not a method — say draft, edit-in-place, or feedback-only, and mean it.

title: Keeping your own voice
description: AI-drafted text defaults to a smoothed-out, generic register unless it's actually shown what your voice sounds like — and even then, specific quirks need to be named, not assumed.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why AI drafts default to a generic voice rather than inferring the writer's actual one
Supply real writing samples and named quirks to keep AI-assisted writing recognisably yours

contentSections.title: Fluent, but nobody

contentSections.body: A newsletter writer uses AI to draft her weekly update. It's grammatically perfect — and reads like nobody. No jokes, no specific phrasing quirks, none of the first-person texture her regular readers know her by. Three of them reply asking if she's okay.

contentSections.question: Why does AI-drafted text default to a smoothed-out, generic voice instead of picking up your specific one automatically?
contentSections.answer: Without being shown your actual writing, the model has nothing of yours to imitate — it defaults to the most broadly acceptable, statistically average register, which by construction isn't anyone's specific voice, including yours.
contentSections.hint: A vague instruction like “sound like me” gives the model a goal but no material — what would it actually be drawing on?

contentSections.body: “Voice” is a specific, nameable thing: word choices you default to, how long your sentences tend to run, a phrase you reuse, the jokes you make, what you leave out entirely. None of that is inferable from a topic or a one-line instruction like “make it sound like me” — it has to come from somewhere. The model can imitate a voice remarkably well once it has real examples of it. Without them, “sound like me” gets treated the way any vague style instruction does: approximated with the nearest generic register, which is confident, correct, and unmistakably nobody's.

contentSections.scenario: You want an AI draft to sound like you. You're deciding what actually gives it something real to work from.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely help the model produce something in your voice?

items.label: Pasting in two or three things you've actually written recently
Naming a specific habit — e.g. “I always start with a one-line summary before the details”
Describing yourself as “casual and funny”
Adding “make it sound human” to the prompt
Saying “warm but professional” as the desired tone

explanation.paste-samples: This is the actual material — real sentences the model can draw specific patterns from, not a description of a pattern.
explanation.name-quirk: A concrete, specific habit is something the model can actually follow, unlike a vague adjective.
explanation.describe-vibe: “Casual and funny” describes a category of voice, not yours specifically — thousands of different actual voices fit that description.
explanation.sound-human: This nudges away from stiff phrasing in general, but gives no information about which specific human voice is wanted.
explanation.say-tone: A tone label narrows the register slightly but still describes a category, not your actual sentences — it's the same problem as “casual and funny.”

contentSections.synthesis: Real samples and specific, nameable habits give the model something to actually imitate. Adjectives and vibe words describe a category of voice that thousands of people share — they narrow the search, but they can't produce yours specifically.

contentSections.body: Voice isn't guessed from a vague instruction — it's built from real samples of your actual writing and named, specific habits.

contentSections.title: Editing toward you, not toward generic-good

contentSections.body: The same newsletter writer pastes in three old posts this time and asks for a draft “in this voice.” Much closer — but it still smooths out her one running bit: a specific nickname for her cat, always dropped in as a mid-sentence aside. The draft mentions the cat. It drops the aside.

contentSections.scenario: The model was given real samples containing the running joke, and still flattened it in the new draft.
contentSections.question: Why would voice-matched output still lose a specific, repeated quirk like this?

options.label: A model optimizing for fluent, coherent prose treats an idiosyncratic mid-sentence interruption as noise to smooth over, not signal to preserve, unless told explicitly to keep that kind of thing
It didn't actually read the three samples closely enough to notice the joke existed
Cats specifically get filtered out of drafts for being too informal a topic

feedback.smoothing: This is the actual pattern — fluency and “correctness” pull toward smoother prose by default, and an aside that interrupts a sentence reads, to that optimization, like something to clean up rather than something load-bearing to your voice.
feedback.didnt-read: The mention of the cat shows the samples were used — the joke's specific delivery (a mid-sentence interruption) is what got lost, not the fact of the cat itself.
feedback.cat-filter: There's no topic-based filter operating here — the issue is structural (an interrupting aside gets smoothed), not about the subject matter.

contentSections.mechanism: Fluency-optimized drafting treats deliberate imperfections — interruptions, asides, repeated bits — as things to clean up unless explicitly told those are the point, not the noise.

contentSections.body: The practical fix has two parts. First, name the specific quirks you want kept, not just “sound like me” from samples alone — “keep the asides, even the ones that interrupt a sentence” is something the model can actually follow. Second, treat the AI draft as raw material for your final pass, not a finished product — read it once specifically hunting for the places your actual habits got sanded down, and put them back yourself. That second step matters even when the first one is done well; it's the one degree of smoothing that's genuinely hard to fully prevent in advance.
Even a voice-matched draft smooths specific quirks by default — name what to keep, and do one pass hunting for what got sanded off.

title: Feedback on your writing that's actually useful
description: Default AI feedback trends toward praise-first and vague — useful feedback has to be asked for specifically: a named failure mode, a named reader, and permission to skip the compliments.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise why default AI feedback trends toward vague praise
Word a feedback request that produces specific, usable criticism

contentSections.title: “Strong, well-written” and nothing else

contentSections.body: A job seeker asks an AI tool for feedback on her cover letter. Back comes: “This is a strong, well-written cover letter! Consider adding more specific metrics to strengthen your impact.” It's not wrong. It's also not useful — it doesn't say what's actually weak, or where a hiring manager would stop reading.

contentSections.question: Why does default AI feedback trend toward praise-first, even on writing with real, fixable problems?
contentSections.answer: Feedback phrasing in training data skews toward softening criticism, and a bare “what do you think” doesn't specify what kind of scrutiny is wanted — so the model defaults to the socially safe version: lead with something positive, offer one mild, generic suggestion.
contentSections.hint: If nothing in the request specifies how harsh to be, which response is less likely to upset anyone: specific criticism, or general praise plus a soft suggestion?

contentSections.body: Vague requests get vague, praise-leaning answers by default — that's not a flaw specific to feedback, it's the same ambiguity problem from lesson 1, showing up in a form that's easy to mistake for real signal because it sounds encouraging. Feedback that actually helps has to be asked for with the same specificity as a draft or an edit: name the failure mode you're checking for (“is this generic,” “does this bury the actual ask,” “would this confuse someone with no context”), name a reader to evaluate against (“a hiring manager who reads 200 of these a week”), and explicitly give permission to skip the compliments. None of that guarantees harsh feedback — it guarantees specific feedback, which is the part that was actually missing.

contentSections.code:
Prompt: “What do you think of this cover letter?”
Output: “This is a strong, well-written cover letter! Consider adding more specific metrics.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw — in the prompt, not in the letter?

options.label: The prompt asks for an opinion with no named criterion or reader — it invites the safest, most generic possible response instead of ruling that response out
AI tools are simply incapable of giving specific feedback on cover letters
Cover letters are too short for any tool to say much about them

feedback.no-criterion: Right — “what do you think” leaves the door wide open for a safe, generic answer. Naming a specific thing to check for or a specific reader closes that door.
feedback.incapable: The second pod of this lesson shows the same tool giving sharp, specific notes once asked the right way — the capability is there, the request just didn't call for it.
feedback.too-short: Length isn't the constraint — a three-sentence cover letter opener has plenty in it to critique specifically once the request asks for that.

contentSections.flawExplanation: “What do you think” is the feedback equivalent of “make this better” from lesson 1 — a goal with no method attached, resolved by default toward the response least likely to sound harsh.

contentSections.body: “What do you think?” invites the safest possible answer — name a failure mode and a reader if you want a useful one.

contentSections.title: Asking sharply, and pushing back on vague praise

contentSections.body: Same job seeker, reworded: “Skip anything positive. Tell me the three weakest sentences in this and why a hiring manager reading 200 of these this week would skip past this one.” The reply names an actual sentence that buries her strongest qualification behind two sentences of throat-clearing. She fixes it in ninety seconds.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding which prompt additions actually tend to produce sharper, more usable feedback.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely sharpen the feedback you get?

items.label: Naming a specific reader and their situation (“a hiring manager reading 200 of these”)
Explicitly asking it to skip anything positive
Asking for the worst three specific things, not a general impression
Asking “is this good?”
Asking for a score out of 10 with no stated criteria

explanation.name-reader: A specific reader with a specific situation gives the model an actual standard to evaluate against, instead of a generic notion of “good.”
explanation.skip-praise: This directly removes the default that produced the vague, praise-first answer earlier in the lesson.
explanation.worst-n: A fixed, small number of specific weak points forces concrete answers instead of a general vibe.
explanation.good-question: This is exactly the open, criterion-free question that produced the vague answer at the start of the lesson.
explanation.score: A number with nothing behind it is a specificity illusion — a 6/10 with no explanation is no more actionable than “strong, well-written.”

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern from lesson 1 holds here too: specificity in the request, not politeness or length, is what produces specificity in the answer. A number or a compliment can both feel like feedback while carrying no actual information to act on.

contentSections.body: One more habit worth building: treat unearned-sounding praise as a signal to ask again, not as confirmation. If you get “this is great, just polish X” on something you suspect has real problems, follow up directly: “If you had to find three real problems with this, not just polish suggestions, what would they be?” That question is hard for a model to answer with more empty praise — it forces a specific list, even from an answer that started out safe.
If the feedback sounds like a compliment with a garnish, ask again and force a specific list — don't take the compliment as the verdict.

title: Difficult emails and messages you're dreading
description: AI is genuinely useful for unsticking the message you've been avoiding — but the register and exactly what you disclose are judgment calls only you get to make, and the model will happily invent detail you never said.

learningObjectives.text: Identify where AI drafting of an emotionally loaded message can go wrong beyond generic voice
Draft a dreaded message that states its own tone and disclosure boundary explicitly

contentSections.title: The excuse you never actually gave

contentSections.body: Someone needs to email a friend to cancel plans for the third time this month — a flare, not an emergency — and has been avoiding writing it for four days. They ask an AI tool to draft it. It comes back apologetic and warm, and includes: “I've been dealing with a hospitalization.” They haven't been hospitalized. It was a bad day on the couch.

contentSections.question: What's the specific risk with AI-drafted difficult messages, beyond the generic-voice problem from lesson 2?
contentSections.answer: Emotionally loaded drafts are exactly where a plausible-sounding, invented detail is most costly — the model fills a gap in the explanation with whatever sounds appropriately serious for the apology it's writing, and “hospitalization” is simply a more narratively complete excuse than “a bad day,” with nothing in the process checking whether it's true.
contentSections.hint: The fabrication mechanism from an earlier phase of this track applies here too — what's the model actually doing when it invents a specific reason?

contentSections.body: For a message like this, AI is genuinely useful for the part that's actually hard when you're tired: getting a structural draft unstuck, so you're editing something instead of staring at a blank message for the fifth day running. What it isn't equipped to decide is the register — how apologetic, how much explanation you actually owe this specific friend, how much detail is true. Default politeness settings will guess, and the guess can be wrong in either direction: oddly clinical when warmth was needed, or over-apologetic to the point of sounding more alarming than the situation is. And as the hook shows, it can also just invent a detail that sounds like it belongs, whether or not it happened.

contentSections.code:
Draft, generated from the prompt “write an apologetic message canceling plans again”: “I'm so sorry — I've been dealing with a hospitalization and haven't been able to get to my phone. I hate doing this to you again.”
Reality: a bad flare day at home, nothing hospital-related.
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw here?

options.label: The prompt never supplied what actually happened, so the model filled the gap with a plausible-sounding, more dramatic reason — which is not the same as lying, but produces the same result if sent unedited
The AI is being deliberately dishonest on the user's behalf
There's no real problem — a slightly exaggerated excuse is a normal, harmless thing to send a friend

feedback.filled-gap: Right — asked for an apologetic explanation with no real reason supplied, the model produced a plausible one. That's the same shape-completion pattern from earlier in this track, just applied to a personal message instead of a citation.
feedback.deliberate: There's no intent here, deliberate or otherwise — the model has no access to what actually happened and generated something that fit the requested tone.
feedback.harmless: A friend who later learns “hospitalization” wasn't true — especially from someone managing a chronic condition, where trust about what's actually happening matters — is a real cost, not a harmless white lie the sender even chose to tell.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The prompt supplied a tone (apologetic) but not the actual facts, so the model invented facts that fit the tone. Anything specific in a drafted message — what happened, why, how bad — has to come from you, or it's a guess dressed as a fact.

contentSections.body: If you didn't supply the actual reason, the model will supply a plausible one — check every specific claim in a difficult-message draft before it goes out.

contentSections.title: Deciding the disclosure boundary out loud

contentSections.body: A harder case: someone needs to ask their manager to leave early for a medical reason and isn't sure how much to say. One AI draft over-explains — naming the specific appointment type unprompted. Another is so vague (“something came up”) that it reads as evasive rather than private.

contentSections.scenario: Two drafts of the same request to a manager: one names more medical detail than the sender wanted to share, the other is vague enough to raise more questions than it answers.
contentSections.question: What's the better way to get a draft that lands where the sender actually wants it?

options.label: State the exact disclosure boundary in the prompt itself — e.g. “Say only ‘a medical appointment,’ nothing more specific” — rather than letting the model guess how much is appropriate
Always pick the more detailed version, since more context reads as more honest
Always pick the vaguer version, since less medical information shared is always safer

feedback.state-boundary: This is the actual fix — the right amount of disclosure is a decision about your specific relationship with your manager, not something the model can infer. Naming the exact line (“a medical appointment,” no more) gets a draft that matches it directly.
feedback.more-detail: More detail isn't inherently more honest — it's a decision about what you're comfortable sharing with a specific person in a specific role, and oversharing to a manager can create problems the sender didn't intend (this gets its own lesson in the admin-life module).
feedback.always-vague: Too vague can read as evasive and prompt more questions, not fewer — the goal isn't maximum privacy by default, it's matching the disclosure you actually intend.

contentSections.concept: The right amount of disclosure in a message is a judgment call about the specific relationship and situation — name it explicitly in the prompt rather than letting the model's guess (in either direction) stand in for your decision.

contentSections.body: The general move: before drafting anything you're dreading, decide out loud — in the prompt — what you will and won't say, and let that boundary be as short as “just say ‘a medical appointment,’ don't elaborate.” This lesson is about the message-specific version of that decision; a later module in this track covers the broader question of what medical and personal information is safe to put into an AI tool in the first place, which matters even before you get to what the message itself says.
For a message you're dreading, AI's job is unsticking the structure — the tone and exactly what you disclose are decisions only you get to make, so state them in the prompt.

title: What you should still write yourself
description: Some writing's value is that doing it yourself is part of what it communicates — recognising which specific piece of a task carries that weight, and getting structural help around it without outsourcing it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify categories of personal writing where AI drafting costs something worth keeping
Use AI for structural help on a personal message without outsourcing the sentiment itself

contentSections.title: It read fine. That was the problem.

contentSections.body: Someone uses AI to draft every message for a month, including a condolence note to a friend whose parent had died. It's warm, correctly worded, nothing factually wrong with it. The friend says months later, gently, that it had felt a little like a form letter.

contentSections.question: What's actually lost when AI drafts something like a condolence note — even a well-edited one, in the sender's own voice?
contentSections.answer: Part of what a message like this communicates is that the sender sat with it and found their own words — the reader usually can't tell whether that's true from the text alone, but for some messages the sender knowing it's true, or not, is the actual point, and a fluent draft can't manufacture that even when it reads perfectly.
contentSections.hint: The friend didn't say it was badly written — she said it felt like a form letter. What does a form letter lack that has nothing to do with grammar or warmth?

contentSections.body: This doesn't apply to everything emotionally loaded — a routine “sorry I'm late” doesn't carry this weight, and drafting it is fine. It applies to a specific, nameable set of cases: grief and condolence messages, an apology for something you actually did wrong, a personal essay or story about something you actually lived through, a reference or recommendation that asserts your own firsthand judgment of someone. What these share is that the ask is implicitly “did you personally do the work of thinking about this” — and outsourcing that specific work is a different thing from outsourcing the sentence-level phrasing, even when the final text looks identical either way.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding which of these belong on the “write it yourself” list — not because AI drafting produces bad writing, but because part of the point is that you personally did the thinking.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely carry that weight?

items.label: A condolence message to a close friend
A real apology for something you did that hurt someone
A recommendation letter asserting your firsthand judgment of a former colleague
A routine message rescheduling a call
A weekly status update to your team

explanation.condolence: Part of what this message says is “I sat with this” — that's the point being communicated, not just the words.
explanation.apology: A real apology asserts that you personally reckoned with what you did — a fluent apology you didn't write carries a different, weaker claim underneath the same words.
explanation.reference: This one specifically claims your own firsthand judgment — letting a model construct that judgment misrepresents whose assessment it actually is.
explanation.reschedule: Nothing about this message implicitly claims personal emotional effort — it's purely logistical, and drafting help costs nothing here.
explanation.status: Routine and repeated — the value of a status update is the information in it, not evidence that you personally agonized over the phrasing.

contentSections.synthesis: The dividing line isn't 'is this emotional' — it's whether part of what the message says is 'I personally did this,' where the model doing it instead quietly changes what's actually true.

contentSections.body: Ask what a message is actually for — if part of the point is proving you did the thinking, that's the part to do yourself.

contentSections.title: Structural help without outsourcing the sentiment

contentSections.body: Someone writing that condolence note next time still wants help — not with what to say, but with not knowing how to start, or whether what they've written is too long, or landing wrong in tone. They don't want the sentiment written for them. They do want to not stare at a blank page.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways to ask for help on a genuinely personal note. (A) “Write a condolence message for a friend whose father died recently.” (B) “I've written a few sentences below. Don't rewrite the sentiment or add anything I didn't say — just tell me if the length feels right and if any sentence reads as more about me than about her.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual difference in what's being outsourced between (A) and (B)?

options.label: (A) hands over the whole task, including deciding what to actually say; (B) keeps the sentiment entirely the sender's own and asks only for structural feedback on something already written
There's no real difference — both are equally “using AI to write a condolence message”
(B) is worse because it takes more effort from the sender for no real benefit

feedback.structural-only: Right — (B) keeps the part that matters (the actual words, the fact that the sender wrote them) entirely theirs, and asks the model only for the kind of help that doesn't touch that: is the length right, does anything read wrong. That's structural help, not sentiment help.
feedback.no-diff: The difference is exactly what's being decided by whom — (A) has the model deciding what to say; (B) has the sender deciding that and only asking for a read on execution.
feedback.worse: The effort is the point, not a cost — for the specific category of message from the first pod, the sender doing the actual thinking is what the message is partly for.

contentSections.concept: “Using AI on a personal message” isn't one thing — asking it to generate the sentiment and asking it to check the length or tone of sentiment you already wrote are different tasks with a very different cost to what the message ends up meaning.

contentSections.body: In practice: for the category of writing from the first pod, it's reasonable to still ask for help with structure — “is this too long,” “does the opening feel abrupt,” “does any sentence read as more about my own feelings than hers” — as long as the actual sentiment stays something you wrote, not something generated and then lightly touched up. The test is simple: if you deleted the AI's involvement entirely, would the message still say something true about whether you did the thinking? For structural-only help, yes. For a generated draft edited into your voice, not really.
Structural help — length, clarity, whether a line lands wrong — is fine even on the writing you should do yourself. Generating the sentiment is the part to keep.

title: Practice — Improve Seven Pieces of Your Own Writing
description: Seven drills applying the draft/edit/critique distinction, voice preservation, sharp feedback requests, and the write-it-yourself line to new scenarios. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's five skills to new writing scenarios without new instruction

contentSections.title: Seven scenarios, seven judgment calls

contentSections.body: Same drill, seven times, with the details changed: a writing scenario, and the question of exactly which of this module's moves actually applies — not a vague instinct, but the specific mechanism from the lessons.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the exact pattern to watch for the next time you draft, edit, or ask for feedback for real.

title: Lab — Rewrite Something Real of Yours, With the Process Logged
description: Take a real piece of your own writing through an AI edit, then go line by line and mark every change as an improvement, a flattening, or a wash — producing a final version you actually stand behind.

learningObjectives.text: Get a bounded AI edit of real personal writing rather than an unbounded rewrite
Judge each specific change an AI edit made against your own actual voice and intent

contentSections.title: Edit it, don't just accept it

contentSections.body: Find something real you've already written — a work email you sent this month, a post, a cover letter paragraph, a message to a friend. Not a hypothetical. Something with your actual sentences in it, that you'd recognise as yours.

contentSections.title: A before-and-after with a logged note on what improved and what flattened
contentSections.brief: Pick a real piece of your own writing, at least a paragraph long. Get an AI tool to edit it — not rewrite it from scratch — using a specific, bounded prompt (per lesson 1: name what may change). Then go through the result change by change and judge each one against your actual intent and voice, not against whether the new version simply reads more smoothly.
contentSections.deliverable: The original text, the exact prompt you used, the AI's edited version, and a line-by-line log marking every meaningful change as an improvement, a flattening, or a wash — each with a one-line reason — plus a final version you actually stand behind.

stages.title: Get a bounded edit, not a rewrite
stages.instructions: Paste in your real text. Write a prompt that names the specific job (edit, not draft or full rewrite) and the boundary of what may change, the way lesson 1 describes. Get the result. Don't judge it yet — just capture the original, the exact prompt, and the output.
stages.checkpoint: You have your original text, your exact prompt, and the AI's edited version, all saved.

stages.title: Judge every change, line by line
stages.instructions: Compare the original and the edit sentence by sentence. For every place they differ, mark it improvement (genuinely clearer or better, and you'd keep it), flattening (a specific quirk, phrase, or piece of your actual voice got smoothed away, per lesson 2), or wash (different, but not clearly better or worse either way). Write one honest sentence for each mark explaining why.
stages.checkpoint: Every difference between the original and the edit has a mark and a one-line reason — including at least one you're marking as a flattening, if one exists, rather than accepting every change as an improvement by default.

stages.title: Build the version you'd actually send
stages.instructions: Starting from the AI's edit, restore anything you marked as a flattening back to your original wording (or something closer to it), and keep the genuine improvements. Write a short closing note: overall, did this edit save you real time, and what's the one thing you'll watch for next time you ask for an edit like this.
stages.checkpoint: You have a final version built from judged pieces of both texts, not the AI's output accepted wholesale, plus a short honest closing note.

rubric.criterion: The prompt asked for a bounded edit, not an open rewrite
rubric.meets: The exact prompt used names the specific job (edit) and states what may or may not change, per lesson 1.

rubric.criterion: Every meaningful change between original and edit is accounted for
rubric.meets: A reader could go sentence by sentence through both versions and find no meaningful difference left unmarked.

rubric.criterion: At least one change is honestly marked as a flattening, if one genuinely occurred
rubric.meets: The log doesn't default to marking every change an improvement — if a specific phrase, quirk, or piece of voice was lost, it's named as such, not smoothed over in the writeup too.

rubric.criterion: The final version is actually assembled from judged pieces, not the raw AI output
rubric.meets: At least one place in the final version differs from the AI's edit because you restored something you marked as flattened.

rubric.criterion: The closing note is a specific, honest assessment
rubric.meets: It names something concrete — real time saved or not, and one specific thing to watch for next time — rather than a general 'AI is helpful' summary.

contentSections.body: The real test of an AI edit isn't whether it reads more smoothly — it's whether you can point to what it changed and still recognise the result as something you'd actually send.

title: Checkpoint — Writing With It
description: Ten questions, all drawn from this module — the first module of this phase, so there's nothing earlier in the phase yet to pull from. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the draft/edit/critique distinction, voice preservation, sharp feedback requests, disclosure boundaries, and the write-it-yourself line without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Writing With It
contentSections.framing: This module opened the phase, so every question here pulls from it — the spaced pulls from earlier modules start next checkpoint.

questions.from: This module — Drafting, editing and critique are three different asks
questions.prompt: “Make this better” with a full draft pasted in is ambiguous because:

options.label: It states a goal but not a method, so the model has to guess between editing in place and rewriting from scratch
The model can't tell the difference between good and bad writing
It's actually unambiguous — it always means a full rewrite

questions.explanation: The prompt names an outcome (better) without naming a method (how much may change), leaving the model to fill that gap — often toward the more thorough-looking rewrite.

questions.from: This module — Drafting, editing and critique are three different asks
questions.prompt: What's the practical fix for getting the specific one of draft/edit/critique you actually want?

options.label: Name the method explicitly — draft from bullets, edit-in-place with a stated boundary, or feedback-only with no rewrite
Always ask for the most thorough option to be safe
Repeat the request multiple times until it works

questions.explanation: Naming the method — not just the goal — removes the ambiguity that causes the model to guess, in either direction.

questions.from: This module — Keeping your own voice
questions.prompt: Why does AI-drafted writing default to a generic voice rather than your specific one?

options.label: Without real samples of your writing, there's nothing specific for the model to imitate, so it defaults to the most broadly acceptable register
Models are incapable of imitating any individual writing style
Voice only matters in fiction, not in everyday writing

questions.explanation: Voice has to come from actual material — samples or named specific habits — not from a topic or a vague instruction like 'sound like me.'

questions.from: This module — Keeping your own voice
questions.prompt: Why can a specific, repeated quirk (like a recurring mid-sentence aside) still get lost even when real writing samples are supplied?

options.label: Fluency-optimized drafting tends to smooth idiosyncratic interruptions as noise unless explicitly told to preserve that kind of thing
The model only reads the first sample provided, ignoring the rest
Quirks longer than one sentence are always dropped automatically

questions.explanation: Samples help enormously but don't guarantee preservation of a deliberate imperfection — naming the specific habit to keep, and a final check pass, still matter.

questions.from: This module — Feedback on your writing that's actually useful
questions.prompt: Why does “what do you think of this?” tend to produce vague, praise-leaning feedback?

options.label: With no named criterion or reader, the model defaults to the socially safest response — general praise plus a mild suggestion
AI tools are incapable of specific criticism
Vague feedback only happens on very short pieces of writing

questions.explanation: The same ambiguity problem from lesson 1 shows up here: an open request gets the safest possible answer by default.

questions.from: This module — Feedback on your writing that's actually useful
questions.prompt: Which combination of prompt additions most reliably sharpens AI feedback?

options.label: Naming a specific reader, asking it to skip praise, and asking for a fixed, small number of specific weak points
Asking for a numeric score with no stated criteria
Simply asking 'is this good?' more than once

questions.explanation: A specific reader, a ban on praise, and a bounded number of concrete weak points together force specificity that a general question doesn't.

questions.from: This module — Difficult emails and messages you're dreading
questions.prompt: What's the specific risk of AI-drafted messages with no real reason supplied?

options.label: The model fills the explanation gap with a plausible-sounding, possibly false, specific detail
The message will always come out too short to be useful
There's no real risk as long as the tone sounds sincere

questions.explanation: The same shape-completion pattern that produces fabricated citations applies here — a plausible detail fills an unsupplied gap, whether or not it's true.

questions.from: This module — Difficult emails and messages you're dreading
questions.prompt: How should you decide how much personal or medical detail a drafted message discloses?

options.label: State the exact disclosure boundary in the prompt itself, rather than letting the model guess
Always choose the most detailed version, since it reads as more honest
Always choose the vaguest version, since less disclosure is always safer

questions.explanation: The right amount of disclosure is a judgment call about a specific relationship — stating it explicitly avoids the model guessing in either direction.

questions.from: This module — What you should still write yourself
questions.prompt: What actually determines whether a piece of writing belongs on the 'write it yourself' list?

options.label: Whether part of what the message communicates is that the sender personally did the thinking, not emotional intensity generally
Whether the topic is sad or difficult
Whether the message is longer than a paragraph

questions.explanation: The dividing line is a specific claim the message makes about who did the work — not how emotional the subject matter is.

questions.from: This module — What you should still write yourself
questions.prompt: Is asking AI for structural feedback (length, whether a line lands wrong) on a condolence note you wrote yourself a violation of the 'write it yourself' idea?

options.label: No — structural feedback on sentiment you actually wrote is different from having the model generate the sentiment itself
Yes — any AI involvement at all defeats the purpose
Only if the feedback changes more than one sentence

questions.explanation: The test is whether the actual sentiment is still the sender's own — structural help around it doesn't change who did the thinking that matters.

title: Summarising a document you provide, versus asking from memory
description: “Summarise this” and “summarise what you know about this” are grounded in completely different ways — one reads the actual text you gave it, the other reconstructs a plausible version from training. They fail differently.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a summary grounded in provided text from one generated from the model's training memory
Get specific figures verified against the actual provided text rather than accepted as summarised

contentSections.title: Two different questions that sound the same

contentSections.body: Someone types “summarise the FMLA rules on intermittent leave” with nothing pasted in. The answer is confident, well-organized, and wrong on one detail that matters — a rule that changed, or one that varies by state and got flattened into one national answer. Nothing in the reply signals that it's working from a blended, uncertain memory rather than reading a specific document.

contentSections.question: What's actually different, mechanically, between “summarise this” with a document pasted in, and “summarise what you know about X” with nothing pasted in?
contentSections.answer: A pasted document sits directly in the model's context — the summary is generated from those actual tokens. “What you know about X” draws on a compressed, blended representation built from many documents seen in training, with no guarantee any part of it matches one specific real document, current rule, or exact figure.
contentSections.hint: One of these has an actual text sitting in front of the model as it writes. Does the other?

contentSections.body: Whenever the real document exists and you can get your hands on it, providing it is strictly safer than asking from memory. A grounded summary can still go wrong — a model can drift from the actual text, or fill a genuinely unclear passage with something plausible-sounding rather than admitting it's unclear — but the errors are bounded and checkable, because there's an actual source sitting right there to check against. A memory-based summary has no such anchor: it might be current, outdated, blended across jurisdictions or versions, or simply wrong, and it will read with exactly the same confident tone either way.

contentSections.code:
Prompt: “What are the eligibility rules for [a specific state disability benefit]?” — no document attached.
Output: a clean, numbered list of rules, stated with total confidence.
contentSections.question: What's the actual risk here, beyond the possibility of a wrong answer?

options.label: There's no way to tell, from the output alone, whether this reflects the current actual rule, an outdated one, or a blend of several similar programs — nothing marks the answer as memory-based rather than grounded
The AI is guaranteed to be wrong about anything related to specific government benefit rules
There's no real risk — confidently stated answers about eligibility rules are reliable by default

feedback.no-marker: Right — the actual danger isn't that this is definitely wrong, it's that there's no signal distinguishing a well-grounded answer from a plausible-sounding, unverified one. Benefit rules change and vary by state; a stale or blended answer looks exactly as confident as a correct one.
feedback.guaranteed-wrong: It isn't guaranteed wrong — plenty of memory-based answers on stable, well-documented topics are fine. The problem is not being able to tell which kind this is without checking.
feedback.no-risk: Eligibility rules for specific programs are exactly the regular-format, long-tail-of-specifics domain from earlier in this track — a strong candidate for confident, unmarked error.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The question asked about a specific, changeable, jurisdiction-dependent rule with nothing provided to ground the answer in — which is precisely the shape of question where memory-based answers are least trustworthy and most confident-sounding regardless.

contentSections.body: If the real document exists, provide it — a grounded summary is checkable against something real; a memory-based one only looks that way.

contentSections.title: Provided doesn't always mean used

contentSections.body: A caregiver pastes in a 40-page benefits handbook and asks for a summary of the deductible and what's covered. The summary sounds right — and states a deductible figure that, on checking, isn't the one written anywhere in the actual handbook. It's a plausible, generic-sounding number for “a plan like this.”

contentSections.scenario: The actual document was pasted in, in full, and the model still produced a specific figure that isn't in it.
contentSections.question: Why would a model substitute a generic figure even with the real document right there in front of it?

options.label: Having seen many similar handbooks in training, the model can substitute a familiar, generic pattern for a specific detail that was oddly phrased, buried, or genuinely hard to locate in the actual provided text, rather than reporting that it couldn't find it
Pasting a document into a prompt doesn't actually give the model access to it
The model deliberately ignores financial figures specifically

feedback.substitution: This is the real pattern — a provided document reduces but doesn't eliminate the shape-completion risk from earlier in this track. Boilerplate-sounding sections are especially prone to this, because the model has seen the generic version of that sentence far more often than this document's specific instance of it.
feedback.no-access: Pasted text is genuinely in context and generally does get used — this isn't an access failure, it's a specific detail getting swapped for a familiar-sounding stand-in.
feedback.ignores-numbers: There's no blanket exclusion of numeric content — the risk is specific to details that are hard to locate or oddly phrased, not to numbers as a category.

contentSections.mechanism: A provided document lowers fabrication risk substantially but doesn't remove it — a specific figure can still get swapped for a plausible, generic one, especially in boilerplate-sounding sections.

contentSections.body: The practical fix: for any figure or specific fact you'll actually act on, ask the model to quote the exact sentence it came from, not just state the number. “Quote the exact sentence stating the deductible” either produces the real quoted text — which you can then check yourself — or exposes that it can't find one, which is itself useful information. Accepting a summarised figure without a location to check is functionally the same risk as the memory-based answer from the first pod, just one layer better disguised.
A pasted document lowers the risk — it doesn't remove it. For any figure that matters, ask for the exact quote it came from, not just the number.

title: Summaries that keep the caveats
description: A summary optimizes for a short, confident-sounding core claim — which is exactly what makes hedges, exceptions and limitations the first thing to get quietly trimmed, even though they can change what the claim is actually licensed to say.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise why summarisation tends to drop caveats, hedges and exceptions specifically
Prompt for caveat-preserving summaries of research and policy documents

contentSections.title: The sentence that didn't make it in

contentSections.body: A study concludes: “These results were observed in a small sample and have not yet been replicated.” The AI summary of it says: “The study found that X improves Y.” Flat, confident, no hedge in sight — a completely different claim than the one the study actually made.

contentSections.question: Why do summaries specifically tend to drop caveats and hedges, rather than dropping detail evenly across a source?
contentSections.answer: Summarising optimizes for a shorter, more confident-reading core claim — and a hedge (“in a small sample,” “has not been replicated,” “in most but not all cases”) is exactly the kind of qualifying, secondary-sounding information that gets treated as trimmable clutter, even though removing it changes what the claim is actually licensed to say.
contentSections.hint: What does a hedge do to a sentence's length and its apparent confidence — and which of those does summarisation usually optimize for?

contentSections.body: This isn't random compression — caveats and hedges are disproportionately likely to be cut because they make a sentence longer and less confident-sounding, which is the opposite of what a good summary is usually optimizing for. “Small sample, not yet replicated” and “this finding held” are very different claims, but a summary trained to sound clean and readable will often flatten the first into the second, because the qualifying half reads like noise rather than like the part that actually determines whether the finding means anything yet. The fix isn't a general instruction to “be careful” — it's a standing, explicit instruction for research and policy summaries specifically: preserve limitations, exceptions and caveats, even if that makes the summary longer or less tidy.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding which prompt additions actually get a caveat-preserving summary rather than a clean-but-flattened one.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely help preserve caveats?

items.label: Explicitly asking: “Include any limitations, caveats, or exceptions the source states, even if it makes this longer”
Asking for caveats to be listed separately from the main claims, not folded into flowing prose
Just asking for “an accurate summary”
Asking for a shorter summary so nothing important gets buried
Asking for the summary to sound authoritative

explanation.explicit-ask: This directly names the thing that tends to get cut and explicitly permits the length cost of keeping it.
explanation.separate-list: Separating caveats out removes the pressure to smooth them into the main narrative, where they're most likely to get trimmed for flow.
explanation.be-accurate: “Accurate” doesn't specify accurate about what — a summary that states the core finding correctly while dropping its caveat can still look, and even be, accurate on its own narrow terms.
explanation.shorter: This is backwards — a shorter target gives the model more reason to cut exactly the qualifying detail this lesson is about, not less.
explanation.confident-tone: This actively pushes in the wrong direction — a confident tone is precisely what a hedge-preserving summary can't have if it's being honest about the source.

contentSections.synthesis: General instructions to be accurate or brief don't target caveats specifically — they either say nothing about them or actively push against keeping them. Only an explicit, specific instruction reliably preserves them.

contentSections.body: Caveats get cut first because they make a summary longer and less confident — ask for them explicitly, or expect them gone.

contentSections.title: The exception clause nobody flagged

contentSections.body: A workplace policy document says accommodation requests are usually processed within two weeks, “except during the annual enrollment period, when processing may take up to six weeks.” Someone submits a request during enrollment, relying on an AI summary that only mentioned “two weeks.” The exception clause never made it into the summary.

contentSections.code:
Source policy: “Requests are typically processed within two weeks, except during the annual enrollment period (Nov–Dec), when processing may take up to six weeks.”
Summary: “Accommodation requests are processed within two weeks.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this summary, specifically?

options.label: It drops a stated exception clause entirely, converting a conditional rule (two weeks except when) into an unconditional one — a materially different claim, not just a shorter version of the same one
It's technically fine — two weeks is the more common case, so leading with it is reasonable
The summary is too short to be useful at all

feedback.dropped-exception: Right — this isn't a length problem, it's a correctness problem. “Two weeks, except when X” and “two weeks” are different claims, and someone relying on the second version during the exception period gets actively misled, not just under-informed.
feedback.fine-common-case: Leading with the common case is fine — silently dropping the exception clause entirely is not the same thing as leading with the typical figure while still stating the exception.
feedback.too-short: Length isn't the issue — a one-sentence summary that included the exception clause would still be short and would be correct.

contentSections.flawExplanation: An exception clause changes the actual rule under specific, real conditions — dropping it doesn't shorten the truth, it replaces a conditional claim with a flatly wrong one for anyone in the excepted situation.

contentSections.body: How much this matters is proportional to what the summary is being used to decide — the same principle from earlier in this track about verifying in proportion to the stakes. A dropped caveat in a summary you're reading out of curiosity costs little. A dropped exception clause in a policy you're about to act on, during exactly the excepted period, can cost real time or a missed deadline. When a summary is feeding directly into a decision with a deadline or a real consequence attached, it's worth explicitly asking: “are there any exceptions or conditions attached to this rule?” — a targeted question, not a general re-read.
A dropped exception clause isn't a shorter version of the truth — it's a different, wrong claim. Ask for exceptions directly when a summary feeds a real decision.

title: Comparing several sources
description: A readable comparison is itself an optimization pressure — the same smoothing tendency from writing a draft can flatten a real disagreement between sources into an apparent, tidy agreement.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise when a source comparison has smoothed over a genuine disagreement between sources
Prompt for a comparison that surfaces disagreement and source quality instead of erasing it

contentSections.title: When 'compare these' erases the disagreement

contentSections.body: Two insurance plan documents cover the same procedure. One states it's covered with prior authorization; the other states it's excluded outright for the same diagnosis code. Asked to “compare these two policies,” the AI's answer reads as if the two plans broadly agree on coverage — the actual conflict never gets named.

contentSections.question: Why might a comparison flatten a genuine disagreement between two sources into something that reads like agreement?
contentSections.answer: Producing a coherent, readable comparison is its own pull toward a tidy narrative — the same smoothing tendency that flattens a specific voice into a generic one in drafting shows up here as flattening a specific conflict into apparent consensus, because a clean resolved-sounding answer reads as more helpful than one that says 'these actually disagree.'
contentSections.hint: This is the same mechanism from the writing module's voice lesson, applied to facts instead of phrasing — what did smoothing do there?

contentSections.body: “Compare these” is itself an underspecified request, the same way “make this better” was in the writing module — it names a goal (a comparison) without naming what to do when the sources genuinely conflict. Left open, the model tends to resolve that ambiguity toward the reading that produces the more coherent-sounding output, which can mean quietly picking one source's version, blending both into something neither actually says, or describing them as more aligned than they are. None of that is deliberate misrepresentation — it's the comparison-specific version of the same shape-completion pull that shows up throughout this track.

contentSections.code:
Source A: “Covered with prior authorization for this diagnosis.”
Source B: “Excluded for this diagnosis.”
Output: “Both plans provide coverage for this procedure, though specific requirements vary.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this comparison?

options.label: It converts a real, direct conflict (covered vs. excluded) into a vague statement (“requirements vary”) that reads as agreement — the disagreement itself never gets named
The output is fine — 'requirements vary' is a reasonable way to summarise any comparison
The flaw is that the AI should have picked which policy is correct

feedback.flattened: Right — 'requirements vary' is technically not false, but it erases the actual finding: these two sources don't just have different requirements, they make opposite coverage decisions. That's the disagreement a real comparison needs to surface, not smooth over.
feedback.fine: It reads smoothly, which is exactly the trap — smooth and accurate aren't the same thing when the underlying sources genuinely conflict.
feedback.should-pick: The model has no way to know which policy actually governs a specific person's situation — the job of a comparison is to surface the conflict clearly, not resolve it by picking a winner.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The comparison had a real, binary conflict to report — covered versus excluded — and instead produced language vague enough to read as consensus, which is worse than either source alone because it actively hides that a decision needs to be made about which one applies.

contentSections.body: 'Compare these' doesn't say what to do when sources disagree — ask explicitly where they conflict, and to quote each one.

contentSections.title: Comparing more than two, and comparing quality too

contentSections.body: Someone gathers three articles about a treatment approach — one from a peer-reviewed journal, one from a hospital patient-education page, one from a wellness blog — and asks for “the overall picture.” The answer blends all three into one summary with no sense that they carry very different weight.

contentSections.scenario: You're comparing several sources of very different quality and want the comparison to actually reflect that, not treat them as equally weighted inputs.
contentSections.question: Which of these prompt approaches genuinely surface both disagreement and quality differences between sources?

items.label: Asking for a table with each claim attributed to its specific source, side by side
Explicitly asking it to flag anywhere the sources differ or disagree
Asking it to note what kind of source each one is (peer-reviewed study, patient page, blog) alongside each claim
Asking for “the consensus view” across all three
Asking “which one is right?” with no further guidance

explanation.table-attributed: Attributing each claim to its specific source keeps the comparison honest about which source actually said what, instead of blending them into one voice.
explanation.flag-differ: This directly targets the exact failure from the first pod — naming disagreement instead of letting it get smoothed into vague agreement.
explanation.name-source-type: Naming source type gives you, the reader, the information needed to weight the claims yourself — a peer-reviewed study and a wellness blog shouldn't be read as equally authoritative.
explanation.consensus: 'Consensus' presupposes agreement exists and asks the model to find or manufacture it, which is exactly the smoothing pressure this lesson warns about, now invited on purpose.
explanation.which-right: Deciding which source is right is a judgment call about source quality and your specific situation — asking the model to just pick one, with no criteria given, hands that judgment away rather than informing it.

contentSections.synthesis: A comparison across sources of different quality needs two things a plain 'compare these' doesn't reliably produce: attribution (which source said what) and an explicit instruction to surface disagreement rather than resolve it.

contentSections.body: When sources differ in quality, ask for attribution and source type, not a blended 'overall picture' — you decide the weighting, not the model.

title: Search-connected tools and what changes
description: A search-connected AI tool fixes staleness — it can find something published after its training ended. It does not fix source-quality judgment, and it can cite a low-quality source with exactly the same confident tone as a high-quality one.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what search-connectivity actually fixes from what it doesn't
Independently check the actual quality and date of a cited source rather than trusting the summary of it

contentSections.title: What search fixes, and what it doesn't

contentSections.body: Someone uses a search-connected assistant to check current guidance on a workplace policy question. It answers confidently and cites a source. The source turns out to be a forum post from a person repeating something they'd heard, not an official or authoritative page — cited with exactly the same tone as if it had been one.

contentSections.question: What does giving an AI tool live web search actually fix, and what does it leave unfixed?
contentSections.answer: It fixes staleness — the tool can find and read something published after its training data ended, which the memory-only mode from lesson 1 structurally cannot do. It does not fix judgment about source quality: the tool still has to decide what counts as reliable when it searches, and it can confidently cite a low-quality source (a forum post, an outdated reprint, an unofficial summary) with the same tone it would use for an authoritative one.
contentSections.hint: Search solves a specific, narrow problem — recency. Does finding a more recent page say anything about whether that page is any good?

contentSections.body: A search-connected tool works by running a search, pulling in snippets or pages from the results, and generating an answer grounded in that retrieved text rather than (only) training memory — which is a real and useful difference from the memory-only mode in lesson 1. But it introduces its own specific risks: it can cite a real, findable, but low-quality or unreliable source, exactly the way a person skimming search results might click the wrong link; it can blend retrieved snippets with older training memory without flagging which is which; and it can get confused about dates — a page that was merely last modified or re-shared recently isn't the same as one describing current information. None of these are fixed by the tool having search access at all; they're a different set of things to watch for, not fewer things.

contentSections.code:
Query: “What's the current guidance on returning to work after this specific medical leave?”
Output: a confident answer, citing a page found via search — which turns out to be a five-year-old forum thread that has been re-indexed and appears recent in search results.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure here?

options.label: The tool treated a findable, recent-looking search result as equivalent to a current, authoritative one, without checking the source's actual reliability or the content's real age
Search-connected tools are incapable of ever finding a genuinely reliable source
The failure is the user's fault for asking about a topic that changes over time

feedback.no-quality-check: Right — search retrieval and quality judgment are two different things. Finding something is not the same as finding something good, and a tool with search access can do the first without reliably doing the second.
feedback.always-bad: Search-connected tools regularly do find and cite genuinely authoritative, current sources — the point isn't that search fails constantly, it's that it can fail confidently, with no built-in signal telling you which case you're in.
feedback.user-fault: Asking about something time-sensitive is exactly the situation search-connectivity is supposed to help with — the failure is in what got cited and how confidently, not in the question being asked.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Live search access changes what the model can retrieve, not how well it judges what it retrieves — a stale or low-quality result can be surfaced and cited with the same unmarked confidence as a genuinely current, authoritative one.

contentSections.body: Search-connectivity fixes staleness, not judgment — a real, findable, cited source can still be a bad one.

contentSections.title: Checking the source it actually cited

contentSections.body: Someone asks a search-connected tool for current guidance and gets a specific cited page. Before acting on it, they click through. The page is a syndicated copy of a much older article, republished on a different site with a “last updated” date that reflects the republishing, not the original guidance.

contentSections.scenario: A search-connected answer cites “healthbenefitsnow.example.com” for a claim about a specific government program's rules.
contentSections.question: What's the single most useful thing to check before trusting this citation?

options.label: Whether this is the actual official source for the program (a government or authoritative page) or a third-party site summarising it, and whether the date reflects the actual rule's currency
Whether the domain name sounds official
Nothing — a citation with a real, working link is sufficient on its own

feedback.check-authority: This is the actual check that matters — a working, real link tells you a page exists, not that it's the authoritative source or that it's current. Third-party sites can accurately summarise official rules, or they can repeat outdated or mistaken versions, and there's no way to tell which from the citation alone.
feedback.domain-sounds: A domain name sounding official is exactly the kind of cheap, easy-to-produce signal this track has repeatedly warned isn't evidence — plenty of unofficial sites have official-sounding names.
feedback.link-enough: A real, clickable link only proves the page exists — it says nothing about whether it's the authoritative source or whether its content is current, which is the actual question.

contentSections.concept: A citation with a real link is a starting point for verification, not the verification itself — the source still has to be checked for actual authority and actual currency.

contentSections.body: The one habit that meaningfully closes this gap: when a search-connected answer matters, ask for the specific source and the actual link for each claim, then spend the thirty seconds to glance at the source itself, not just the model's summary of it — checking who published it, whether it reads like an official or authoritative page versus a forum, blog, or aggregator, and whether the date attached to it is a genuine original publish date or just a “last modified” stamp from a reshare. This is the same targeted-verification move from earlier in this track, applied specifically to the new failure mode search introduces: verify the source, not just the claim.
A real, clickable citation proves a page exists — it doesn't prove it's authoritative or current. Check both before you act on it.

title: Reading enough of the original to catch a wrong summary
description: You don't need to read the whole document to catch a bad summary — you need to read the specific part behind the one or two claims you're actually about to act on.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which specific claims in a summary are worth direct verification against the original
Locate and read the targeted section of a source behind a decision-driving claim

contentSections.title: The one number that mattered

contentSections.body: Someone gets an AI summary of a 40-page benefits report and acts on it without reading any of the original — a reasonable-sounding choice, since reading all 40 pages was exactly what they were trying to avoid. Weeks later, one number in the summary turns out to be wrong, and it was the number the whole decision rested on.

contentSections.question: What's the actual minimum viable check for a long-document summary you're about to rely on — not reading it all, but not nothing either?
contentSections.answer: Not the whole document, and not zero — the specific section behind the one or two claims the decision actually depends on. Most of a long document's content doesn't carry any real decision weight; the check that matters is targeted at exactly the part that does, not distributed evenly across all forty pages.
contentSections.hint: Of everything in a 40-page report, how much of it is actually load-bearing for the one decision being made right now?

contentSections.body: This is the same proportional-verification idea from earlier in this track, applied specifically to long documents rather than short claims: identify which one or two things in the summary you're actually going to act on, ask the model to point you to exactly where in the source those come from (a page number, a section heading, a quoted sentence), and read just that part yourself. This takes minutes, not hours, and it catches the exact failure from the hook — a summary that's fine everywhere except the one place that mattered, which a full read would catch too, at a cost most people won't actually pay, and a spot-check aimed at the wrong part wouldn't catch at all.

contentSections.scenario: You have 40 pages and five minutes before you need to act on the AI summary's key claim. You're choosing a verification strategy.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually has a real chance of catching an error in the specific claim you're relying on?

items.label: Asking where in the source the key claim comes from, and reading that specific section
Reading just the first page of the original document
Skimming the table of contents
Reading only the document's conclusion section, regardless of where the key claim actually lives
Searching the original document for the specific number or term the claim depends on

explanation.targeted-section: This is the direct version of the fix — go to exactly where the claim is supposed to come from and check it there.
explanation.read-first-page: The first page is the least likely place for a decision-critical, specific detail buried deep in a 40-page report to actually live — this checks the wrong part.
explanation.skim-toc: A table of contents tells you the document's structure, not whether a specific stated figure is accurate.
explanation.read-conclusion: A conclusion may restate a headline finding without including the specific figure or caveat your decision actually depends on — useful for other things, not targeted at this.
explanation.search-keyword: Searching the original for the actual term or number is a fast, direct way to locate and check the specific claim, especially in a digital document.

contentSections.synthesis: A useful spot-check in a long document isn't about reading more of it randomly — it's about locating the exact part the decision-critical claim is supposed to come from and checking that specific part.

contentSections.body: You don't need to read the whole document — you need to find and read the specific part behind the one claim your decision actually rests on.

contentSections.title: One spoon, one claim

contentSections.body: Same 40-page report, a much lower-energy day. There's enough focus for exactly one targeted check, not several. The summary has eight distinct factual claims in it.

contentSections.scenario: A summary of a 40-page document contains eight distinct factual claims. You have the energy for exactly one targeted verification before you have to decide whether to act on the summary.
contentSections.question: Of those eight claims, how many actually need direct verification for this one check to meaningfully protect the decision you're making?
contentSections.explanation: Usually just one — the specific claim the actual decision hinges on, not a representative sample across all eight. Verifying a claim that isn't load-bearing for your decision protects nothing, no matter how thoroughly you check it; verifying the one that is protects the whole decision, even if the other seven go unchecked. On a low-energy day, picking correctly which one that is matters more than checking more than one.

contentSections.body: This is the bad-day version of the same skill, not a lesser one: when there's only capacity for one check, spend it identifying which single claim the decision actually depends on, then verify that one directly — “point me to exactly where in the source this figure comes from” is a fast enough question to ask even on a foggy day. A partial check aimed at the right claim beats a thorough-feeling skim of the wrong parts, and it beats trusting the summary wholesale because a full read wasn't available. The skill isn't reading more — it's aiming better.
On a low-capacity day, one well-aimed check beats a longer, unfocused one — spend your one check on the claim the decision actually depends on.

title: Practice — Assess Seven Summaries Against Their Sources
description: Seven drills applying grounded-versus-memory summaries, caveat preservation, source comparison, search-tool citation checking, and targeted verification to new scenarios. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's five skills to new research and summarising scenarios without new instruction

contentSections.title: Seven summaries, seven checks

contentSections.body: Same drill, seven times, with the details changed: a summary or a source-comparison, and the question of exactly what to check before relying on it — not a vague instinct, but the specific mechanism from this module's lessons.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the exact pattern to watch for next time you rely on a real AI summary.

title: Lab — Summarise a Long Real Document and Verify It
description: Take a real, long document you actually need summarised, get a grounded and caveat-preserving summary, then trace every claim in it back to a specific location in the source.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a grounded, caveat-preserving summary of a real long document
Trace every claim in a summary to a specific, checkable location in the source

contentSections.title: Summarise it, then prove it

contentSections.body: Find a real, long document you actually have a reason to want summarised — a lease, a benefits handbook, a policy document, a long research article, terms of service you're about to agree to. Something with enough length and enough specific claims in it that reading the whole thing is genuinely the thing you're trying to avoid.

contentSections.title: A summary with every claim traced to a location in the source
contentSections.brief: Pick a real document at least several pages long. Get a grounded, caveat-preserving AI summary of it — provided in full, not asked from memory, with explicit instructions to keep limitations and exceptions. Then go through every specific, checkable claim in the summary and locate exactly where in the source it comes from, marking anything you can't locate.
