contentSections.deliverable: The summary, with every specific claim in it annotated with its exact source location (a page, section, or quoted sentence) or marked as unlocatable, plus a short closing note on how many claims held up, how many didn't, and whether any caveat from the original was dropped in the first-pass summary before you caught it.

stages.title: Get a grounded, caveat-preserving summary
stages.instructions: Provide the full document (not a description of it) and write a prompt that asks for a summary explicitly preserving caveats, exceptions and limitations, per lesson 2. Save the exact prompt and the resulting summary.
stages.checkpoint: You have the full source document, your exact prompt, and the resulting summary, all saved.

stages.title: List and locate every specific claim
stages.instructions: Go through the summary and list every specific, checkable claim it makes — a number, a date, a rule, an exception. For each one, ask the model to point you to exactly where in the source it comes from (a page, section, or quote), then check that location yourself in the actual document.
stages.checkpoint: Every specific claim in the summary has a located source position you've personally checked, or is marked as unlocatable.

stages.title: Check for dropped caveats and write the honest summary
stages.instructions: Re-read the original document's caveats, exceptions and limitations directly, and check each one against your AI summary — was it kept, or dropped even after you asked for caveat preservation? Write a short closing note: how many claims held up on checking, how many didn't, and whether anything in the original's limitations got lost anyway.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written list of the original's stated caveats cross-checked against the summary, and a short honest closing note.

rubric.criterion: The summary was grounded in the actual provided document, not asked from memory
rubric.meets: The full source document was pasted or uploaded before the summary was requested, per lesson 1.

rubric.criterion: The prompt explicitly asked for caveats, exceptions and limitations to be preserved
rubric.meets: The exact prompt used names this requirement directly, per lesson 2, not just 'be accurate.'

rubric.criterion: Every specific claim is traced to a real, checked location in the source
rubric.meets: A reader could go through the annotated summary and find a page, section, or quote backing every specific claim — or an honest 'unlocatable' mark where one doesn't exist.

rubric.criterion: Dropped caveats are checked for directly, not assumed absent
rubric.meets: The original's stated limitations and exceptions were read directly and compared against the summary, not just trusted to have carried over.

rubric.criterion: The closing note is a specific, honest tally
rubric.meets: It states real numbers — how many claims held up, how many didn't, whether any caveat was lost — not a general impression.

contentSections.body: A summary you can trace, claim by claim, back to the actual document is a genuinely different, more trustworthy thing than one you simply believe because it reads well.

title: Checkpoint — Research and Summarising
description: Ten questions: six from this module, four reaching back to Writing With It — the only earlier module in this phase so far. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve grounded-versus-memory summarising, caveat preservation, source comparison, search-citation checking, and targeted verification without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Research and Summarising

questions.from: This module — Summarising a document you provide, versus asking from memory
questions.prompt: Why is a summary of a document you actually provided structurally safer than one asked from memory?

options.label: It's generated from the real text in context, rather than a blended, possibly outdated representation with no guarantee of matching any specific real document
Both are equally reliable, since both are stated confidently
Memory-based summaries are always clearly labeled as such

questions.explanation: A provided document gives the model actual text to ground the summary in; a memory-based answer has no such anchor and carries no visible marker distinguishing it from a grounded one.

questions.from: This module — Summarising a document you provide, versus asking from memory
questions.prompt: Even with the real document provided, what should you still do before acting on a specific stated figure?

options.label: Ask for the exact quote it came from and check that it's genuinely in the source
Nothing further — a provided document guarantees every detail is accurate
Ask a second AI tool the same question in the same conversation

questions.explanation: A provided document lowers but doesn't remove fabrication risk — quoting and checking the exact sentence catches a substituted, generic-sounding figure.

questions.from: This module — Summaries that keep the caveats
questions.prompt: Why do summaries tend to drop caveats and hedges specifically, rather than trimming evenly?

options.label: A hedge makes a sentence longer and less confident-sounding, which is the opposite of what summarisation is usually optimizing for
Caveats are usually factually incorrect, so removing them improves accuracy
Hedges only appear in documents too technical for AI tools to process

questions.explanation: Caveats are exactly the qualifying, secondary-sounding content that a compression process treats as trimmable, even though removing them changes the claim.

questions.from: This module — Comparing several sources
questions.prompt: Why might a comparison of two conflicting sources describe them as being in general agreement?

options.label: A coherent, readable comparison is its own pull toward a tidy narrative, which can smooth a real conflict into apparent consensus
The model always picks the more recently published source as correct
Sources that use different wording are always treated as disagreeing, even when they agree

questions.explanation: The same smoothing tendency that flattens voice in drafting can flatten a genuine factual conflict into a vague, agreement-reading statement.

questions.from: This module — Search-connected tools and what changes
questions.prompt: What does giving an AI tool live web search access actually fix?

options.label: Staleness — it can retrieve information published after its training data ended
Source-quality judgment — it can now reliably distinguish authoritative sources from unreliable ones
Nothing meaningful changes with search access

questions.explanation: Search-connectivity solves the recency problem specifically — it doesn't add reliable judgment about whether a found source is actually good.

questions.from: This module — Reading enough of the original to catch a wrong summary
questions.prompt: What's the right target for a spot-check on a long-document summary you're about to act on?

options.label: The specific section behind the one or two claims the decision actually depends on
The first page of the original document
An even sample spread evenly across the entire document

questions.explanation: A targeted check aimed at the decision-critical claim protects the actual decision — an evenly spread or front-loaded sample doesn't reliably land on the part that matters.

questions.from: This module — Reading enough of the original to catch a wrong summary
questions.prompt: On a low-capacity day with room for exactly one verification check, what should determine which claim you check?

options.label: Which single claim the actual decision you're making depends on
Whichever claim appears first in the summary
Whichever claim sounds the most surprising

questions.explanation: One well-aimed check on the decision-critical claim protects the decision; a check aimed at an interesting but non-load-bearing claim protects nothing.

questions.from: Previous module — Writing With It
questions.prompt: Why is “make this better,” with a draft pasted in, an ambiguous instruction?

options.label: It states a goal but not a method, leaving the model to guess between editing in place and rewriting from scratch
It's unambiguous — it always means a light edit
The ambiguity only matters for very long documents

questions.explanation: Naming the method — edit, draft, or critique — removes an ambiguity that “make this better” leaves entirely open.

questions.from: Previous module — Writing With It
questions.prompt: Why can a specific writing quirk still get lost even when real samples of your voice are provided?

options.label: Fluency-optimized drafting treats idiosyncratic interruptions or asides as noise to smooth unless told explicitly to keep them
The model can only process one sample at a time
Quirks are always preserved once any real samples are given

questions.explanation: Samples help substantially but don't guarantee preservation of a deliberate imperfection — naming the specific habit to keep still matters.

questions.from: Previous module — Writing With It
questions.prompt: What determines whether a piece of writing belongs on the “write it yourself” list, per that module?

options.label: Whether part of what it communicates is that the sender personally did the thinking, not how emotional the topic is generally
Whether the topic involves loss or grief specifically
Whether the message is longer than one paragraph

questions.explanation: The dividing line is a specific claim the message makes about who did the work, not the emotional intensity of the subject matter.

title: Explanations at the level you're actually at
description: “Explain this simply” doesn't say what you already know — it names a vague target level instead of your specific one, and the model guesses, often wrong in either direction.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why 'explain simply' doesn't reliably calibrate to a specific learner's actual background
State existing knowledge explicitly to get an explanation pitched at the right level

contentSections.title: Simply for who?

contentSections.body: Someone new to spreadsheets asks “explain VLOOKUP” and gets an answer full of terms — array arguments, exact-match parameter — that assumes knowledge they don't have yet. Someone else, already comfortable with formulas, asks a follow-up question and gets “explain like I'm 5,” with a balloon-and-basket analogy standing in for an answer they could have handled directly.

contentSections.question: Why doesn't “explain this simply” reliably produce an explanation pitched at your actual level?
contentSections.answer: “Simply” names a direction (less complex) but not a destination — it says nothing about what you already know, so the model has to guess a default level, and that guess can land too basic for someone with adjacent knowledge or too advanced for a true beginner, with nothing in the request to correct it either way.
contentSections.hint: Two people with very different backgrounds could both reasonably ask for something 'simple' — would they mean the same thing?

contentSections.body: The fix isn't a stronger version of “simple” — it's stating what you actually already know, which gives the model something concrete to calibrate against instead of a guess. “I know Excel formulas like SUM and IF, but I've never used a lookup function” tells it exactly where to start and what not to re-explain. This works in either direction: a true beginner names that explicitly instead of getting a jargon-dense default aimed at someone further along, and someone with real adjacent knowledge names that too, instead of getting a condescending от-the-basics explanation of something they already understand most of.
State what you already know — that's the actual calibration signal “explain simply” is missing.

contentSections.title: The same question, wildly different depth

contentSections.body: Someone managing a new diagnosis wants to understand a term their doctor used, without either sounding like they're spiraling into internet self-diagnosis or getting a flattened pop-science version that skips the part they actually need. The exact same question, asked slightly differently, gets back either a dense clinical answer or an oversimplified one — never quite the useful middle.

contentSections.scenario: Two near-identical questions about the same medical term: one phrased casually (“what does X mean”) gets a simplified, vague answer; one that includes a specific clinical word the person picked up from their doctor gets a much denser, jargon-heavy one.
contentSections.question: Why would such a small phrasing difference produce such different depth?

options.label: Absent an explicit statement of background, the model infers your level from cues in your own phrasing — which word choices you use, what you already mentioned — and those cues can point toward either extreme with no reliable in-between
Medical terms specifically always trigger the most clinical possible explanation
The model is randomly inconsistent about depth regardless of phrasing

feedback.infers-cues: Right — using one clinical word can read as a signal of existing medical fluency, even if it's just a term picked up secondhand from a doctor's visit, and the model calibrates depth to that cue rather than to your actual background.
feedback.medical-triggers-clinical: It's not the topic that decides this — the casual phrasing of the same term got a simplified answer, so the mechanism is about the phrasing cues, not the subject matter.
feedback.random: There's a real, findable mechanism here — the two answers differ because of specific cues in how the question was asked, not chance.

contentSections.mechanism: In the absence of stated background, the model reads calibration cues out of your own word choice — which is an unreliable substitute for actually being told what you know.

contentSections.body: The practical version of the fix from the first pod, applied here: name your actual background directly rather than letting word choice do it by accident — “my doctor used this term, I don't have a medical background, and I want to actually understand it, not just get the simplest possible gloss.” It also helps to close the loop afterward: “does that make sense, or should I go more basic — or more precise?” turns level-calibration into a quick two-way check instead of a one-shot guess.
Don't let incidental word choice signal your level by accident — state it, and check afterward whether the pitch actually landed.

title: Asking it to quiz you rather than tell you
description: Recognising a correct explanation when you read it and producing it yourself from memory are different skills — reading fluently tests the first one, not the second, and only the second is what using the knowledge later requires.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why reading a clear explanation doesn't reliably build the ability to produce or use it later
Request quizzing that forces genuine recall rather than recognition

contentSections.title: Reading it and knowing it are different things

contentSections.body: Someone reads a genuinely clear AI explanation of a concept for work, nods along, feels like it clicked — and then blanks completely an hour later when a coworker asks them to explain the same thing out loud.

contentSections.question: Why doesn't reading a clear explanation reliably transfer into being able to produce or use the concept yourself later?
contentSections.answer: Recognising correct information when you see it, and generating it yourself from memory, are different cognitive skills — reading a fluent explanation is a much easier recognition task, which is why it feels like understanding, but it doesn't exercise the retrieval pathway that explaining or using the concept later actually requires.
contentSections.hint: Multiple-choice questions and fill-in-the-blank-from-scratch feel very different to answer, even on the same material — why?

contentSections.body: This is the testing effect, and it's the same principle behind why this track's own lessons ask you to guess before explaining a mechanism: producing an answer yourself, even a wrong one, builds a stronger and more durable version of that knowledge than reading the right answer does. Reading is a recognition task — you're checking whether each sentence makes sense as you go, which is genuinely easier than generating the same content unprompted. The gap between those two doesn't show up while you're reading; it shows up later, exactly when you actually need the knowledge and there's no explanation in front of you to recognise against.
Reading a clear explanation tests recognition, not recall — and recall is what you'll actually need later.

contentSections.title: Quizzing that actually forces recall

contentSections.body: Someone tries “quiz me on this” and gets a multiple-choice question with four options. It's still mostly a recognition task — pick the answer that looks right out of a short list — not much closer to the blank-page test from the first pod than reading was.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways of asking to be quizzed on the same material. (A) “Quiz me on this with multiple choice questions.” (B) “Give me a scenario and ask me what I'd do, or ask me to explain it back to you — don't give me options, and don't tell me if I'm right until I've actually answered.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual difference in what each one tests?

options.label: (A) is still mostly a recognition task — the right answer is sitting right there among the options; (B) forces you to generate the answer yourself with nothing to recognise it against, which is much closer to what using the knowledge for real requires
There's no real difference — both are equally “quizzing”
(A) is better because it's faster to answer

feedback.generation: Right — a scenario question or an unprompted explain-it-back forces genuine generation, with nothing to recognise the answer against, which is the actual skill reading and multiple-choice both under-exercise.
feedback.no-diff: The label “quiz” covers both, but the underlying cognitive task is very different — recognition versus generation — which is exactly the distinction this lesson is about.
feedback.faster-better: Faster to answer is often a sign it's testing less — the effortful, slower version is frequently the one that's actually building something durable.

contentSections.concept: A quiz request is only as strong as the recall it actually forces — asking for open, scenario-based, or explain-it-back questions with no options and delayed feedback pushes toward genuine generation instead of recognition.

contentSections.body: In practice: ask explicitly for open questions instead of multiple choice, for scenarios (“here's a situation — what would you do, and why”) rather than definitions, and for the model to withhold the answer until after you've actually responded rather than showing options alongside the question. None of this needs to feel like a formal exam — “explain it back to me in your own words and I'll tell you what I'd add” is a perfectly good version of the same move, and it's the one this track's own lessons are built around.
Ask for open, scenario-based questions with the answer withheld — recognition-friendly quizzing barely improves on just reading.

title: The illusion of understanding a good explanation
description: How easy an explanation was to follow and how well you actually understand it feel like the same thing from the inside — and they're not. Fluency is not evidence of depth.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a fluent explanation can feel like understanding without producing it
Identify genuine signs of understanding versus signs that are actually just fluency

contentSections.title: It read clearly. That's not the same thing.

contentSections.body: Someone reads a beautifully clear AI explanation of a concept for a certification exam, nodding along the whole way, feeling genuinely smart. A week later, asked to apply the same concept to a slightly different example with no explanation to read alongside it, they can't do it — and can't even identify what specifically they're missing.

contentSections.question: Why does a fluent, easy-to-follow explanation feel like understanding, even when it isn't yet?
contentSections.answer: The felt ease of processing a smooth explanation and the felt ease of genuinely understanding something are very similar from the inside — low effort while reading gets misread as depth of comprehension, because both produce the same subjective sense of 'this makes sense,' even though one is about how well the text was written and the other is about what's actually in your head afterward.
contentSections.hint: What does it feel like, from the inside, to read something well-written versus to have actually mastered its content? Are those two feelings distinguishable in the moment?

contentSections.body: This is the fluency illusion, and AI explanations are especially good at triggering it because they're reliably well-organized, clearly worded, and free of the confusing tangents a hastily written human explanation might have — all real virtues, and all things that make an explanation easier to follow without making it any more likely you could reproduce or apply the content unaided. The actual test of understanding isn't how the explanation felt while you were reading it — it's whether you can use the concept with the source removed: explain it in your own words from a blank page, apply it to a new example the explanation didn't cover, or answer a question about it days later, not minutes.
How easy an explanation was to read tells you about the explanation, not about what you now know — test with the source removed.

contentSections.title: The tell you can actually notice

contentSections.body: Someone learning a new work skill keeps getting AI explanations that read as completely clear each time — and keeps needing to ask essentially the same question again, worded slightly differently, a few weeks later. Each individual explanation felt like it landed. Nothing was actually accumulating.

contentSections.scenario: You're trying to tell whether your understanding of something is genuine or just repeatedly refreshed fluency.
contentSections.question: Which of these are actual signs of genuine understanding, rather than signs that are really just fluency in disguise?

items.label: You can explain it from a blank page, with no source in front of you
You can apply it correctly to an example the original explanation never covered
You can still answer a question about it correctly several days later, unprompted
The explanation felt completely clear while you were reading it
You didn't have any follow-up questions after reading it

explanation.explain-unaided: This directly removes the recognition scaffold — if you can produce it from nothing, that's genuine evidence, not just felt fluency.
explanation.new-example: Applying a concept to a genuinely new case tests whether you understood the underlying idea or just followed one specific worked example.
explanation.recall-later: Time removes the freshness effect — if it's still there days later, unprompted, that's real retention, not a momentary recognition high.
explanation.felt-clear: This is exactly the fluency signal the lesson warns about — it measures the explanation's quality, not your retained understanding of it.
explanation.no-questions: Having no follow-up questions can mean genuine clarity, or it can mean you didn't understand it well enough yet to know what you'd need to ask — the absence of questions isn't reliable evidence either way.

contentSections.synthesis: The real signs of understanding all involve removing the source and adding either time or novelty — anything that can be true purely because the explanation itself was well-written doesn't count.

contentSections.body: The practical habit: after an explanation that felt clear, deliberately do one of the unaided tests before moving on — close the tab and explain it in your own words, or ask the model for a new example to try it on and check your own answer against its check. Needing to look back at the source, even once, is useful information, not failure — it tells you specifically where the retained understanding stopped, which is exactly the gap a felt-clear reading never reveals on its own.
The real signs of understanding all involve removing the source — feeling clear while reading isn't one of them.

title: Learning from an explanation that might be wrong
description: As a beginner, you have no independent basis to judge whether an explanation is right — which means a wrong foundational concept doesn't just sit there wrong, it gets built on, and gets harder to catch the longer it goes unnoticed.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an incorrect explanation is especially costly when you're a genuine beginner in the topic
Cross-check a foundational or high-stakes explanation against a second, independent source

contentSections.title: The wrong thing you build on for weeks

contentSections.body: A student learns a plausible-sounding but subtly wrong explanation of a core concept early in a course, and keeps using it, confidently, for weeks — it explains everything they've encountered so far well enough that nothing has contradicted it yet. Unlearning it later costs far more than getting it right the first time would have.

contentSections.question: Why is a wrong explanation especially costly specifically when you're a genuine beginner learning it, compared to when you already know the topic?
contentSections.answer: As a beginner you have no independent basis to notice something's off — an expert reading the same wrong explanation might catch an inconsistency against what they already know, but a beginner has nothing to check it against yet, so the error doesn't just sit there: it becomes the foundation later understanding gets built on top of, and it gets harder to catch and unlearn the longer that continues.
contentSections.hint: An expert reading a wrong explanation might feel something's off. What would a true beginner feel reading the exact same wrong explanation?

contentSections.body: This connects directly to something from earlier in this track: confidence in how an explanation is phrased is not evidence of its correctness, and a model has no separate honesty check running underneath a fluent-sounding wrong explanation any more than it does for a fabricated citation. What's specific to the learning context is the compounding — a wrong number in an isolated fact stays a wrong number, but a wrong foundational concept quietly reshapes how you interpret everything that follows it, and there's no felt “that's off” signal to catch it, because feeling that something is off requires already knowing enough to notice the inconsistency — which is exactly what a beginner doesn't have yet.
A wrong foundational concept doesn't stay a small error — you build on it, and you have no way to notice until it's already load-bearing.

contentSections.title: When a second source is worth the extra ten minutes

contentSections.body: Someone learning a new skill for work is about to teach a colleague what they just learned from an AI explanation — a genuinely good moment to notice they've never actually checked it against anything else.

contentSections.code: Situation: learned a core concept from a single AI explanation, never checked elsewhere, about to (a) build a decision on it, or (b) explain it to someone else as fact.
contentSections.question: What's the actual risk being taken here, specifically?

options.label: The concept is being treated as verified when it's only been checked against a single, unconfirmed source — and it's about to be built on or passed to someone else in exactly the way that makes an undetected error compound
There's no real risk — a clear AI explanation is reliable enough to teach from directly
The only risk is wasting time double-checking something that's probably fine

feedback.unverified-foundation: Right — the two situations named (building a decision on it, or passing it to someone else as settled fact) are exactly where an unverified foundational error does the most damage, and exactly where a ten-minute second check is proportionate, not excessive.
feedback.no-risk: Clarity of phrasing isn't evidence of accuracy — this is the exact confusion this track has repeatedly warned against, now showing up in a learning context.
feedback.wasted-time: For a foundational concept about to be built on or taught to someone else, the cost of a compounding, undetected error is generally much higher than ten minutes spent checking a second source.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The risk isn't that the explanation is definitely wrong — most of the time it probably isn't. It's that nothing has confirmed it's right, and it's about to be treated as if something had.

contentSections.body: The proportional heuristic: the newer the concept is to you, the more foundational it is to everything you'll learn after it, and the more consequential it is if wrong — the more worth a quick cross-check against a second, independent source before you build on it or teach it forward. That doesn't mean fact-checking every single explanation; it means specifically checking the ones you're about to rely on, the same proportional-verification principle from earlier in this track, applied here to what you're learning rather than what you're doing.
Cross-check the concepts you're about to build on or teach forward — that's where an unverified foundational error does the most damage.

title: Using it on a foggy day without it doing the thinking
description: Passive reading on a low-capacity day can feel like productive studying while requiring almost no real capacity — which means it can quietly waste the limited energy you did spend, rather than genuinely saving it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why passive AI-assisted reading on a low-energy day can cost more than it appears to
Structure a low-energy study session that still involves genuine retrieval

contentSections.title: The studying that doesn't cost anything, and doesn't build anything

contentSections.body: On a genuinely foggy day, someone wants to keep learning something without the energy for real effortful retrieval. They let AI explain everything, read along passively, and feel like they got some studying done. A week later, on a clearer day, none of it seems to have actually stuck.

contentSections.question: On a low-capacity day, is passive reading actually the lower-cost choice compared to a small amount of active retrieval — or does it cost something specific of its own?
contentSections.answer: Passive reading produces the fluency illusion from earlier in this module — it feels like productive studying — while requiring almost no real cognitive engagement, which means the limited energy that was spent on it produced little retained understanding. It isn't free just because it felt easy; it's a real spend of limited capacity on something that mostly doesn't build anything durable.
contentSections.hint: The energy spent reading passively still counts as spent — what did it actually buy?

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument against resting — choosing not to study at all on a bad day is a completely legitimate choice, and forcing effortful learning through a genuinely foggy day isn't the point here. It's specifically about the case where some capacity is going to be spent on learning today regardless: a small amount of genuine retrieval effort tends to produce more retained value for the same or even less energy than passive reading does, because passive reading's main cost is time and attention with little to show for it, while a short retrieval attempt — even a failed one — does something reading alone doesn't.
Passive reading on a low-energy day isn't free just because it feels easy — it's capacity spent with little retained in return.

contentSections.title: Knowing when to actually stop

contentSections.body: Same foggy day, further in. The concept is hard to hold onto, and it's not clear anymore whether that's the normal difficulty of learning something new, or a sign that today just isn't a day this can happen.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a study-session structure that fits a genuinely low-energy day and still involves real retrieval, not just reading.

fields.prompt: How much new material to attempt
options: As much as a normal session would cover
fields.feedback: Narrowing scope is what makes real engagement affordable on a low-energy day — one concept done with genuine retrieval beats several done passively.

fields.prompt: What happens before the AI explains the concept
options: A quick attempt at what you think it means first
Nothing — go straight to the explanation
fields.correctValue: A quick attempt at what you think it means first
fields.feedback: A retrieval attempt before the explanation, even a wrong one, does more than reading straight through — this is the predict-first move this module keeps coming back to.

options: Say it back in one sentence, unaided, right now
Move on once the explanation feels clear
fields.correctValue: Say it back in one sentence, unaided, right now
fields.feedback: This is the one honest signal that something actually landed — 'it felt clear' is the fluency illusion from earlier in this module, not evidence.

contentSections.synthesis: A study cycle this short still works, as long as it keeps the two things a longer passive read tends to skip: an attempt before the answer, and an unaided check after it.

contentSections.body: A low-energy study structure that still involves genuine engagement doesn't need to be elaborate — one single concept, a retrieval attempt before any explanation, and one very short recall check at the end, said back with nothing in front of you. And the honest stopping signal, if it comes to that: not “this concept is hard” — real learning is often supposed to feel effortful, that's not itself a reason to stop — but “I genuinely can't tell whether any of this is registering.” When that's the actual state, closing the tab is the correct bad-day accommodation, not giving up. There will be a clearer day to pick it back up; there usually isn't a version of pushing through today that produces anything worth having kept.
One concept, an attempt before the answer, an unaided check after — that's a complete low-energy cycle. Stop when nothing's registering, not when it's merely hard.

title: Practice — Convert Seven Passive Study Asks Into Active Ones
description: Seven drills applying level-calibration, recall-forcing quiz requests, the fluency illusion, cross-checking foundational concepts, and low-energy study structure to new scenarios. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's five skills to new learning scenarios without new instruction

contentSections.title: Seven study habits, seven fixes

contentSections.body: Same drill, seven times, with the details changed: a passive or miscalibrated way of studying with AI, and the question of exactly which of this module's moves turns it into something that actually builds understanding.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the exact study habit worth changing this week.

title: Lab — Learn One Topic Using AI and Prove You Learned It
description: Pick a real topic you don't yet understand, learn it using this module's active techniques, then produce a written explanation entirely unaided — the actual test of whether it stuck.

learningObjectives.text: Apply level-calibration and active-retrieval techniques to genuinely learn a new topic
Produce an unaided explanation that demonstrates real, not illusory, understanding

contentSections.title: Learn it, then close the tab and prove it

contentSections.body: Pick a real topic you genuinely don't understand yet, and would actually benefit from learning — something for work, a hobby, or a decision you're facing. Not something you already half-know. The whole point of this lab is starting from real unfamiliarity and ending with something you can prove, unaided.

contentSections.title: A written explanation of the topic in your own words, unaided
contentSections.brief: Choose a real topic you don't currently understand. Use AI to learn it, applying this module's techniques: state your actual background so the explanations calibrate correctly, ask to be quizzed with open, generation-forcing questions rather than reading passively, and cross-check anything foundational against a second source. Then, with no AI tool or source open, write out your own explanation of the topic from memory.
contentSections.deliverable: A short log of how you learned the topic (what you asked, what quizzing looked like, what you cross-checked), followed by a genuinely unaided written explanation of the topic in your own words — written with no source open — plus a short honest note on what the unaided writing revealed that felt shaky, even if the learning sessions had felt clear.

stages.title: Calibrate and learn actively
stages.instructions: State your actual existing background on the topic so the AI's explanations calibrate correctly, per lesson 1. As you learn, ask to be quizzed with open, scenario-based or explain-it-back questions rather than multiple choice, per lesson 2 — don't just read passively.
stages.checkpoint: You have a log of your starting background, the explanations you got, and at least one round of genuine open-ended quizzing you attempted.

stages.title: Cross-check anything foundational
stages.instructions: Identify the one or two most foundational claims in what you learned — the ones everything else depends on — and check them against a second, independent source, per lesson 4.
stages.checkpoint: You've named the foundational claim(s) and checked them against something other than the original AI explanation.

stages.title: Close every source and write it from memory
stages.instructions: With no AI tool, no notes, and no source material open, write a genuine explanation of the topic in your own words — enough that someone unfamiliar with it could follow. Afterward, note honestly where you got stuck, had to guess, or realized you didn't actually know something you thought you did.
stages.checkpoint: You have a genuinely unaided written explanation, plus an honest note on where the writing revealed gaps the earlier learning sessions hadn't.

rubric.criterion: The learning process used explicit level-calibration, not a vague 'explain simply'
rubric.meets: The log shows your actual stated background being used to pitch the explanation, per lesson 1.

rubric.criterion: At least one round of genuine, generation-forcing quizzing happened
rubric.meets: The log shows an open or scenario-based question you attempted to answer yourself, not just multiple choice or passive reading.

rubric.criterion: A foundational claim was cross-checked against a second source
rubric.meets: At least one core claim is checked against something other than the original AI explanation, with a note on what was found.

rubric.criterion: The final explanation was written with genuinely no source open
rubric.meets: The explanation reads as produced from memory, including natural gaps or imprecision, not as a lightly reworded copy of the original explanation.

rubric.criterion: The closing note honestly names what the unaided writing revealed
rubric.meets: It identifies something specific that felt shaky or uncertain in the unaided version, even if the earlier learning sessions had felt completely clear.

contentSections.body: The learning sessions can feel clear the whole way through — the unaided page is where you actually find out what you know.

title: Checkpoint — Learning With It
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to Research and Summarising, two reaching further back to Writing With It.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve level-calibration, recall-forcing quizzing, the fluency illusion, foundational cross-checking, and low-energy study structure without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Learning With It
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four reaching back one module to Research and Summarising, two reaching further back to Writing With It.

questions.from: This module — Explanations at the level you're actually at
questions.prompt: Why doesn't “explain this simply” reliably calibrate to your specific level?

options.label: It names a direction, not a destination — it says nothing about what you already know, so the model has to guess
The word 'simply' is always interpreted identically by every model
It works fine for beginners but never for advanced learners

questions.explanation: Stating your actual existing knowledge gives a real anchor to calibrate against — 'simply' alone doesn't.

questions.from: This module — Asking it to quiz you rather than tell you
questions.prompt: Why does reading a clear explanation not reliably build the ability to use the concept later?

options.label: Reading is a recognition task, while producing or using the concept later requires recall — a different, harder skill
AI explanations are usually inaccurate, which is the real problem
Reading and recall are the same skill, so this generally isn't a real gap

questions.explanation: Recognition and generation are different cognitive tasks — reading fluently exercises the easier one.

questions.from: This module — The illusion of understanding a good explanation
questions.prompt: What's a genuine sign of understanding, as opposed to a sign that's really just fluency?

options.label: Being able to apply the concept to a new example the original explanation never covered
The explanation feeling completely clear while reading it
Having no follow-up questions after reading

questions.explanation: Genuine signs remove the source and add novelty or time — felt clarity while reading measures the explanation, not your retention.

questions.from: This module — Learning from an explanation that might be wrong
questions.prompt: Why is a wrong explanation especially costly when you're a true beginner in the topic?

options.label: A beginner has no independent basis to notice the error, so it becomes the foundation later understanding gets built on
Beginners are simply less careful readers than experts
It isn't more costly — experts and beginners are equally likely to catch it

questions.explanation: Noticing an inconsistency requires prior knowledge to compare against, which a true beginner doesn't yet have.

questions.from: Previous module — Summarising a document you provide, versus asking from memory
questions.prompt: Why is a summary of a provided document structurally safer than one asked from memory?

options.label: It's grounded in the actual provided text, rather than a blended, possibly outdated representation from training
Memory-based summaries are always clearly labeled as uncertain
Both are equally reliable regardless of grounding

questions.explanation: A provided document gives real text to ground the summary in; memory-based answers have no such anchor.

questions.from: Previous module — Summaries that keep the caveats
questions.prompt: Why do AI summaries tend to drop caveats and hedges specifically?

options.label: Hedges make a sentence longer and less confident-sounding, which summarisation is usually optimizing against
Caveats are usually inaccurate, so dropping them improves the summary
Hedges are dropped only from documents longer than 20 pages

questions.explanation: Caveats are exactly the qualifying content that gets treated as trimmable in the pursuit of a shorter, confident-sounding core claim.

questions.from: Previous module — Comparing several sources
questions.prompt: Why might a comparison of two genuinely conflicting sources be described as if they broadly agree?

options.label: A coherent, readable comparison pulls toward a tidy narrative, which can smooth a real conflict into apparent consensus
The model always defaults to whichever source was provided first
Genuine disagreements between sources are extremely rare in practice

questions.explanation: The same smoothing pull that flattens voice in drafting can flatten a real factual conflict into vague agreement.

questions.from: Previous module — Search-connected tools and what changes
questions.prompt: What does live web search access on an AI tool actually fix?

options.label: Staleness — access to information published after the training cutoff
Judgment about whether a found source is authoritative
Both staleness and source-quality judgment equally

questions.explanation: Search-connectivity solves recency specifically — it doesn't add reliable judgment about source quality.

questions.from: Older — Writing With It
questions.prompt: Why is “make this better” with a full draft pasted in ambiguous?

options.label: It names a goal but not a method, leaving the model to guess between light edit and full rewrite
It always means a full rewrite, unambiguously
It's only ambiguous for very short pieces of writing

questions.explanation: Naming the method — draft, edit, or critique — is what removes the ambiguity 'make this better' leaves open.

questions.from: Older — What you should still write yourself
questions.prompt: What determines whether a piece of writing belongs on the 'write it yourself' list?

options.label: Whether part of what it communicates is that the sender personally did the thinking
Whether the topic is sad or emotionally difficult
Whether it's longer than a paragraph

questions.explanation: The dividing line is a specific claim the message makes about who did the work, not general emotional intensity.

title: Letters, appeals and forms you're too tired to write
description: The fatigue itself is often the actual barrier to an appeal or a form getting written at all — a genuinely useful accommodation, as long as every specific fact in the draft comes from you and gets checked, not invented to fill a gap.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise AI drafting of appeals and forms as a legitimate accommodation, not a shortcut that risks the outcome
Supply the specific facts a draft needs and verify them before submitting

contentSections.title: The barrier isn't knowing what to say

contentSections.body: An insurance denial letter needs a response within thirty days. The person it's addressed to knows roughly what needs to be said — but the blank page, on a day when even sitting upright for twenty minutes is a real cost, is the actual barrier. The letter doesn't get written. The deadline gets closer.

contentSections.question: Is using AI to draft an appeal letter a legitimate accommodation for genuinely limited capacity, or a shortcut that risks the outcome of something this consequential?
contentSections.answer: It's a legitimate accommodation, with one real condition attached: appeals have a fairly standard structure, and the actual skill a good one needs — citing the right dates, referencing the specific denial language, stating a clear request — is well within what a draft-and-verify process can produce, as long as every specific fact in the draft is checked against your real records afterward, not assumed correct because it reads convincingly.
contentSections.hint: What's actually hard about writing an appeal letter — knowing the structure, or having the energy to produce it? And does AI drafting change which of those two things is doing the work?

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely different situation from the writing module's “what you should still write yourself” question — an appeal letter doesn't ask “did you personally do the emotional work,” it asks whether the right facts got stated clearly enough, on time, to a specific institution. That's exactly the kind of task where lowering the barrier to getting it written at all matters more than any small cost to it not being in your own literary voice. The condition that makes this safe rather than risky is the same fabrication caution from earlier in this track: the letter's specific facts — dates, policy numbers, what was previously said to you, what you're specifically requesting — have to come from you, and any of them the draft states need checking against your actual records before anything gets sent.
Not having the energy to write it isn't a reason to skip getting it written — it's exactly the situation a checked, fact-verified draft is for.

contentSections.title: Giving it your actual specifics

contentSections.body: Someone asks an AI tool to “write an appeal letter for my insurance denial” with no further detail. The draft comes back fluent and structurally correct — and cites a policy section number that isn't the one in the actual denial letter, because none was given to reference.

contentSections.code:
Prompt: “Write an appeal letter for my insurance denial of a physical therapy referral.”
Output includes: “As stated in Section 4.2 of your policy, this referral meets the medical necessity criteria...”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw here?

options.label: No policy document or denial letter was provided, so “Section 4.2” is a plausible-sounding, invented reference — exactly the citation-fabrication pattern from earlier in this track, now inside a document with real consequences
The AI is being deliberately dishonest about the policy
There's no real flaw — insurance policies commonly have a section like this, so it's a reasonable guess

feedback.invented-citation: Right — this is the exact fabrication pattern from earlier in this track, now showing up inside a document that will actually be submitted. A specific section number was never provided, and the model filled the gap with a plausible-looking one.
feedback.deliberate: There's no intent here — the model has no access to the real policy and generated a citation with the right shape for the request, the same shape-completion process as any other fabrication.
feedback.reasonable-guess: A 'reasonable guess' cited as fact in a formal appeal is exactly the risk — if Section 4.2 doesn't actually say that, or doesn't exist, the appeal cites something false, which can undermine the whole letter's credibility.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The prompt described the situation but never supplied the actual denial letter or policy text, so anything specific the draft states about that document's contents is a guess dressed as a citation.

contentSections.body: The practical fix: paste in the actual denial letter, any referenced policy language, and prior correspondence before asking for a draft, and state the specific outcome you want. Then ask the draft to reference only what was actually provided — and before it goes anywhere, check every specific claim (a policy section, a date, a prior phone call it mentions) against your real records the same way this track has covered for any other AI-drafted document with facts that matter.
Provide the actual denial letter and policy language, not a description of them — and check every specific claim in the draft before it's submitted.

title: Preparing for an appointment: questions and a summary
description: The safe, genuinely useful role for AI before an appointment is organizational — turning your own scattered notes into a short, prioritized summary and question list. Asking it to speculate about what's wrong is a different, much riskier use.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish AI's organizational role in appointment prep from a diagnostic one it shouldn't take on
Produce a length-capped, priority-ordered summary that fits a real appointment's constraints

contentSections.title: Organizing what you already know

contentSections.body: Someone managing a complex, multi-symptom condition has fifteen minutes with a specialist and, every time, leaves having forgotten to mention half of what they'd meant to — or gets overwhelmed mid-appointment and can't retrieve any of it in the moment.

contentSections.question: What's the actual, safe value AI adds to appointment prep — organizing what you already know, or providing new medical judgment about your symptoms?
contentSections.answer: The safe value is organizational: turning your own notes and symptom timeline into a short, prioritized, readable summary, and helping generate a focused list of questions. It isn't a source of medical assessment — asking it to speculate about what might be causing something is a categorically different, much riskier use than asking it to help organize information you already have and want to communicate clearly.
contentSections.hint: One of these uses AI to reshape information you already possess. The other asks it to generate new medical claims about your body. Which one is this lesson actually about?

contentSections.body: In practice: gather your own notes — a rough symptom timeline, what's changed, what you're worried about — and ask specifically for two things: a one-page summary organized by what's most important to raise first, and a short list of specific questions you want answered. Bound the request explicitly to organizing your own information, not assessing it — “help me organize this into something I can hand to my doctor” asks for something safe and genuinely useful; “what do you think is causing this” asks for something this lesson's second pod, and the module's fifth lesson, cover as a different and much riskier request.
AI's job here is organizing what you already know into something a fifteen-minute appointment can actually use — not assessing it.

contentSections.title: The three-page summary nobody can use

contentSections.body: The summary comes back three dense pages long, every symptom given equal weight, nothing prioritized. Handing it to a doctor with fifteen minutes is, if anything, more exhausting than just trying to remember everything out loud would have been.

contentSections.code:
Prompt: “Summarize my symptoms from these notes for my doctor.”
Output: three pages, every symptom and date given equal length and weight, no indication of what matters most.
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw here?

options.label: The request never specified a length constraint or a priority order, so the model produced a summary optimized for completeness rather than for what a real fifteen-minute appointment can actually absorb
The AI is incapable of producing short summaries
Three pages is actually the right length for a medical summary

feedback.no-constraint: Right — 'summarize' alone doesn't say how short, or what to prioritize. Left open, the model defaults toward completeness, which reads as thorough but isn't actually usable inside a real time-boxed appointment.
feedback.incapable: The lesson's own fix shows the same tool producing a tight, prioritized version once asked — the capability is there, the constraint was missing.
feedback.right-length: Length that matches your real time with the clinician is what matters, not length in the abstract — three unprioritized pages is a real, common failure mode for exactly this reason.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Without a stated cap or priority order, 'summarize' produces the most complete-looking version by default, which is the wrong optimization for a document meant to be used inside a short, real conversation.

contentSections.body: The fix is the same specificity move from earlier in this track: name the actual constraint. “One page maximum. List the top three things I most need addressed today first, and put everything else below as background only, in case there's time.” That produces something that respects the real fifteen minutes, instead of a technically complete document that's harder to use than no summary at all.
Name the actual constraint — length and priority order — or you'll get a complete-looking summary that's too dense for the appointment it's for.

title: Understanding a document written to be hard to understand
description: Some dense bureaucratic language is just bad writing — some of it is precise, binding text where the density is a byproduct of real legal weight. An AI paraphrase makes either kind readable, but only one of them is safe to act on as if it were the actual rule.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a readability aid from the actual binding text when a real deadline or consequence is at stake
Extract deadlines and required actions from a dense document with the exact source sentence attached

contentSections.title: Readable isn't the same as authoritative

contentSections.body: A disability benefits denial letter is three pages of dense bureaucratic language. Buried in a subordinate clause on page three, after two pages of boilerplate, is the actual appeal deadline — sixty days, not the ninety a skimmed first paragraph seemed to imply.

contentSections.question: Is a document like this hard to parse purely by accident, or is some of that density doing real work?
contentSections.answer: Both are true at once: plenty of bureaucratic density really is just bad writing, but some legal and insurance language is genuinely precise, and dense as a direct byproduct of that precision, because it's binding text with real legal weight attached to its exact wording — which means an AI simplification of it makes it readable without making the simplified version the actual authoritative text.
contentSections.hint: Why might a document choose exact, complex wording over a simpler version that says almost the same thing — what would 'almost' cost, on a document like this?

contentSections.body: This distinction matters specifically because of what a plain-language AI summary is for: it's a comprehension aid, genuinely useful for understanding what a document is roughly saying, and it is not a substitute for the actual clause when a real deadline, dollar amount, or required action depends on the exact wording. The research module's lesson on quoting exact sentences rather than accepting a paraphrased figure applies here with higher stakes attached — a summarized “about two months to appeal” instead of “sixty days from the date of this notice” is exactly the kind of imprecision that can cost someone a real appeal window.

contentSections.code:
Denial letter (actual text, page 3): “...any request for reconsideration must be submitted in writing within sixty (60) calendar days of the date of this notice.”
AI summary: “You have about two months to appeal this decision.”
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this summary, specifically?

options.label: “About two months” is a looser paraphrase of a precise, binding sixty-calendar-day deadline — close enough to sound right, but not the number the actual clock runs on
There's no flaw — sixty days and about two months are functionally identical
The summary should have been longer to be accurate

feedback.loose-paraphrase: Right — sixty calendar days can be as few as fifty-nine days short of 'two months' depending on the month, and a deadline calculated from the wrong anchor is exactly the kind of gap that costs someone their appeal window. Readable and precise aren't the same thing here.
feedback.no-flaw: They're close, which is exactly the trap — close enough to feel fine, not close enough to safely calculate an actual filing deadline from.
feedback.too-short: Length isn't the issue — a short summary that stated 'sixty calendar days from the date of this notice' would be both short and precise.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A summary can be accurate in spirit and imprecise in exactly the number that determines a real deadline — the fix isn't a longer summary, it's treating any number this consequential as something to quote exactly, not paraphrase.

contentSections.body: A plain-language summary is for understanding a document — for a real deadline or dollar figure, go back to the exact wording, not the paraphrase.

contentSections.title: Extracting what actually needs action

contentSections.body: The same denial letter has, buried across three pages, one actual deadline, two specific documents that need submitting, and one phone number to call for questions. None of that is flagged distinctly — it reads as one continuous block of formal language, easy to read past.

contentSections.scenario: You have a dense, multi-page document and need to know exactly what it's actually asking you to do.
contentSections.question: What's the strongest way to extract the actionable content from it?

options.label: Ask for a structured extraction: every deadline, every required action, and every document needed — each one paired with the exact quoted sentence it comes from, not a paraphrase
Ask for a general summary of what the letter is about
Read the letter once yourself and trust your own read of what needs doing

feedback.structured-quoted: This is the strongest combination — structure separates the actionable items from the surrounding boilerplate, and requiring an exact quote for each one applies the research module's verification habit directly to a document with real personal stakes.
feedback.general-summary: A general summary is exactly what produced the loosely-paraphrased deadline in the first pod — it's useful for gist, not for extracting precise, actionable specifics.
feedback.self-read-only: A single read-through of genuinely dense bureaucratic language is exactly the condition under which a buried deadline or requirement gets missed — that's the problem this lesson opened with, not a fix for it.

contentSections.concept: A structured, quote-anchored extraction turns a dense document into an actionable checklist without losing the precision a plain summary drops.

contentSections.body: In practice: “List every deadline, every document I need to submit, and every action required in this letter. For each one, quote the exact sentence it comes from.” This does two things at once — it surfaces the actionable items that get lost in surrounding boilerplate, and the quote requirement means you're checking the model's extraction against real text, not trusting a summary of a summary. For anything with a real deadline attached, that quoted sentence is the thing to act on, not the extraction's restatement of it.
Ask for a structured list of deadlines and required actions, each with its exact source quote — that's what turns a dense document into something you can actually act on correctly.

title: What never to put in: your data, other people's data
description: Almost nothing about getting help with a document requires the exact identifying string inside it — and when a document contains someone else's private information, the decision about what risk to accept isn't yours to make alone.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which specific details in a personal document are safe to redact before pasting it into an AI tool
Recognise other people's private information in a document as a categorically stricter case than your own

contentSections.title: What the task actually needs

contentSections.body: Someone pastes a full explanation-of-benefits statement into a general-purpose AI chatbot to get the medical billing codes explained — full account number, full home address, and their child's full name and diagnosis, all on the same page, all pasted in along with everything else.

contentSections.question: What's the actual specific risk in pasting a document like this in full, versus a redacted version, into a consumer AI tool?
contentSections.answer: Depending on the specific product and its settings, conversation content may be retained for purposes like model improvement or support — meaning identifying details typed in become a copy of that information sitting somewhere outside your control. The task — explaining what a billing code means — almost never actually requires the account number, the exact address, or a child's full name to be present; a version with those specific strings removed or replaced accomplishes exactly the same task.
contentSections.hint: What does explaining a medical billing code actually require to be present in the text — and does an account number or a child's name have anything to do with that?

contentSections.body: The practical habit is narrower than “never share anything personal” — it's redacting or replacing the specific identifying strings a task doesn't actually need: full account and policy numbers, exact home addresses, full legal names, dates of birth, and any government ID number, replaced with a placeholder or removed outright, while keeping the substantive content the task genuinely depends on — the billing code, the dollar amount, the coverage question, the general nature of the visit. “Explain what code 99214 with a $340 charge typically covers” does the same job as pasting the whole statement, without the account number ever being typed anywhere.
Redact the specific identifying strings a task doesn't need — the account number, the exact address, the full name — and keep the substance the task actually depends on.

contentSections.title: Someone else's information isn't yours to risk

contentSections.body: A caregiver manages both a parent's and a child's medical paperwork alongside their own. Pasting a document to get help with it now routinely means pasting someone else's diagnosis, someone else's account number, someone else's full name — not just their own.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how the redaction habit from the first pod should change when a document contains another person's private information rather than only your own.
contentSections.question: Which of these reflect the actual, stricter standard this situation calls for?

items.label: You can decide your own risk tolerance for your own data, but you don't have the same standing to make that call for someone else's private information
Redact another person's identifying details at least as thoroughly as your own, even if it takes an extra minute
The same redaction standard applies equally, since it's the same kind of information either way
Being a caregiver with legitimate authority to manage someone's paperwork means the usual redaction caution doesn't apply

explanation.not-your-call-alone: This is the actual reason the standard is stricter — consenting to a privacy tradeoff for yourself is a decision only you can make for yourself; making that same tradeoff for someone else, even with good intentions, isn't the same kind of decision.
explanation.redact-more: In practice this usually means treating another person's identifying details with at least the same care as your own, and often more, since they have no way to weigh in on the tradeoff being made.
explanation.same-standard: The category is genuinely different — your own risk tolerance for your own data doesn't transfer to someone else's data just because the type of information looks similar.
explanation.caregiver-exception: Legal or practical authority to manage someone's paperwork is about handling the document — it doesn't extend to deciding, on their behalf and without them, how much of their private information should sit inside a third-party AI tool's history.

contentSections.synthesis: Your own data is a decision you can make about your own risk tolerance. Someone else's data — a family member's diagnosis, a coworker's personal details — isn't a decision that belongs to you alone, even when you're the one holding the document.

contentSections.body: The practical fix is the same redaction habit from the first pod, applied more strictly: when a document contains another person's identifying or medical information, remove it before pasting, even if it's slightly less convenient, and especially don't rely on a general sense that “it's fine, I'm just trying to help them” — the person whose information it is didn't get a say in that decision, and the redaction costs almost nothing compared to what's being protected.
Your own risk tolerance is yours to set. Someone else's private information in a document you're handling isn't your call to risk — redact it, even more carefully than your own.

title: Medical information: what it can help with and where to stop
description: Diagnosis requires a physical exam, lab results, a full history and follow-up over time — information a model structurally cannot get. A good-sounding answer to “what's wrong with me” is a plausible list generated from symptom-pattern text, not a diagnostic process.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why diagnostic questions are structurally different from organizational or educational ones
Recognise a gray-area medical question as one that still requires an actual clinician's assessment

contentSections.title: 'What's wrong with me' is the wrong question to ask it

contentSections.body: Someone with new, worrying symptoms types “what's wrong with me?” into an AI chatbot instead of calling anyone. The answer is a careful-sounding list of possible conditions ranging from minor to serious — technically hedged, but it raises anxiety without providing an actual path to a real answer, because nothing about generating that list involved examining them, ordering a test, or knowing their actual history.

contentSections.question: Why is “what's wrong with me” specifically a worse question to bring to an AI tool than “help me organize this to bring to a doctor” or “should I be concerned enough to seek care today”?
contentSections.answer: Diagnosis requires information the model structurally cannot obtain — a physical exam, lab results, a full history, and often follow-up over time — so an answer to “what's wrong with me” is necessarily a plausible-sounding list generated from matching symptom-pattern text, not an actual diagnostic process. The other two questions ask for something it genuinely can help with — organizing information, or a general framework for urgency — without pretending to replace an assessment it has no way to actually perform.
contentSections.hint: What does a real diagnosis require that a text-based tool structurally cannot access, no matter how detailed the symptom description is?

contentSections.body: The line, stated concretely: genuinely useful uses are organizing your own timeline (this module's second lesson), understanding a term or a document (its third lesson), general educational information about a condition you already have a diagnosis for, and preparing questions to bring to an actual appointment. Not-useful and actively risky uses are asking it to diagnose new symptoms, asking it to decide whether something is serious enough to skip seeking care, or asking it to interpret your own test results as a replacement for the clinician who ordered them and has your actual context. The first set uses AI on information; the second set asks it to substitute for an assessment it cannot perform.
AI can organize what you know and help you ask better questions — it cannot examine you, order a test, or replace the person who can.

contentSections.title: The gray-area case

contentSections.body: Someone with an existing, already-diagnosed condition notices a new symptom and isn't sure whether it's an expected variation of something they already live with, or a departure worth flagging — a genuinely harder case than “diagnose me from scratch,” because it sounds like it's just about understanding their own situation better.

contentSections.scenario: Two versions of a question about the same new symptom in someone with an existing diagnosis. (A) “I have [condition] and I'm noticing [new symptom] — help me understand what questions to ask my doctor about whether this is expected or worth flagging.” (B) “I have [condition] and I'm noticing [new symptom] — should I skip going in, or is this nothing to worry about?”
contentSections.question: What's the actual difference between these two, given this lesson's line?

options.label: (A) asks for help preparing to bring the question to someone who can actually assess it; (B) asks the model to make the same triage decision itself — exactly the assessment it structurally can't perform
Both are equally safe, since both mention an existing diagnosis for context
Both are equally risky, since both involve a new symptom

feedback.prep-vs-triage: Right — (A) stays on the organizational side of the line from the first pod, preparing a better conversation with someone who can actually assess the symptom. (B) asks the model to make the actual triage call, which is precisely the kind of judgment this lesson names as requiring real assessment.
feedback.both-safe: Mentioning an existing diagnosis provides context, but it doesn't change what's actually being asked — (B) is still asking for a decision the model has no way to safely make.
feedback.both-risky: The two questions are meaningfully different in kind — (A) doesn't ask the model to decide anything about the person's actual health status, while (B) does.

contentSections.concept: Even with real context about an existing condition, the deciding factor is whether the question asks for help preparing information, or asks the model to make the assessment itself.

contentSections.body: The practical rule: if the real answer to a question requires someone with your actual full history and the ability to physically assess you, it's not a question for an AI tool to answer directly, no matter how careful and well-hedged the response sounds. A good-sounding answer to a triage-shaped question is a reason to go get an actual assessment sooner, not evidence that one isn't needed — treating it as a substitute is exactly the risk this lesson is naming, dressed up in a genuinely sympathetic, well-organized reply.
If the real answer needs your actual history and a physical assessment, that's not a question for AI — a careful-sounding answer to it is a reason to seek real care sooner, not a substitute for it.
