title: Lab — Draft One Real Piece of Admin, With Privacy Handled
description: Draft a real piece of admin you actually need — a letter, an appeal, a form, an appointment summary — with identifying details redacted first and every specific fact verified before it's considered finished.

learningObjectives.text: Redact unneeded identifying details before requesting AI assistance on a real document
Verify every specific, checkable fact in an AI-drafted piece of admin against real records

contentSections.title: Draft it for real, safely

contentSections.body: Pick a real piece of admin you actually need done — an appeal letter, a benefits form, a landlord letter, an appointment-prep summary, a request for an accommodation. Something with real stakes, not a hypothetical exercise.

contentSections.title: A usable draft plus a note on what you redacted and why
contentSections.brief: Choose one real piece of admin writing you actually need. Identify what identifying detail can be redacted before anything is pasted into an AI tool, per lesson 4. Provide the real supporting material with that detail removed, get a draft, and verify every specific, checkable fact in it against your real records before considering it finished.
contentSections.deliverable: The redacted source material you provided, the exact prompt used, the resulting draft, a list of every specific fact in the draft you checked and how, and a short note on what you redacted and why it didn't cost the draft anything.

stages.title: Redact and gather the real material
stages.instructions: Gather the actual documents or notes this piece of admin needs (a denial letter, symptom notes, a prior message). Identify and remove any identifying detail the task doesn't actually need — account numbers, exact addresses, full names not required for the task — per lesson 4.
stages.checkpoint: You have the real source material with unneeded identifying details redacted, ready to provide.

stages.title: Get the draft
stages.instructions: Write a prompt that provides the redacted real material and states the specific outcome you want, per lesson 1. Save the exact prompt and the resulting draft.
stages.checkpoint: You have your exact prompt and the resulting draft, both saved.

stages.title: Verify every specific fact
stages.instructions: List every specific, checkable claim in the draft — a date, a policy reference, a prior conversation, a requested outcome — and check each one against your real records. Fix anything that doesn't match. Write a short closing note on what was redacted and confirm the draft didn't lose anything it actually needed.
stages.checkpoint: Every specific fact in the draft has been checked and corrected if needed, and you have a short closing note on the redaction.

rubric.criterion: Unneeded identifying details were redacted before anything was submitted to the AI tool
rubric.meets: The redacted source material shows specific identifying strings (account numbers, addresses, unneeded full names) removed, per lesson 4.

rubric.criterion: The draft was grounded in real, provided material, not a vague description
rubric.meets: The exact prompt shows real supporting material was provided, not just a summary of the situation from memory.

rubric.criterion: Every specific, checkable fact in the draft was verified
rubric.meets: A reader could go through the draft and find no specific date, reference, or claim left unchecked against real records.

rubric.criterion: The redaction didn't cost the draft anything it actually needed
rubric.meets: The closing note explicitly confirms the draft still accomplishes its real purpose despite the redacted details being absent.

rubric.criterion: The final draft is genuinely usable, not just technically complete
rubric.meets: The deliverable is something that could actually be sent or submitted as-is, not a draft still requiring substantial rework.

contentSections.body: A usable draft and a safe one aren't in tension — redacting what the task doesn't need and verifying what it does need cost the draft nothing real.

title: Checkpoint — Admin, Health and Life Logistics
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four reaching back to Learning With It, two reaching further back — one each from Writing With It and Research and Summarising.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve fact-checked drafting, organizational appointment prep, readability-versus-authority, data redaction, and the diagnostic line without looking them up

contentSections.title: What stuck
Checkpoint — Admin, Health and Life Logistics
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four reaching back one module to Learning With It, two reaching further back — one each from Writing With It and Research and Summarising.

questions.from: This module — Letters, appeals and forms you're too tired to write
questions.prompt: What makes AI drafting of an appeal letter safe rather than risky?

options.label: Every specific fact in the draft — dates, references, requests — comes from you and gets checked against real records before it's sent
Appeal letters are too formulaic for anything to go wrong
Nothing makes it safe — it should always be avoided for consequential documents

questions.explanation: The accommodation is legitimate specifically because facts are supplied and verified, not because the task is risk-free by default.

questions.from: This module — Preparing for an appointment: questions and a summary
questions.prompt: What's the safe, useful role for AI in appointment prep?

options.label: Organizing your own notes into a short, prioritized summary and question list
Assessing your symptoms and telling you what's likely wrong
Deciding how urgent your situation is

questions.explanation: The safe role is organizational — reshaping information you already have, not generating new medical judgment.

questions.from: This module — Understanding a document written to be hard to understand
questions.prompt: Why is a plain-language AI summary not safe to act on directly for a specific deadline?

options.label: A summary is a comprehension aid, not the binding text — the exact original wording is what a real deadline should be calculated from
AI summaries are always factually wrong
Deadlines are never stated precisely in legal documents

questions.explanation: Readability and authority are different properties — a summary can be clear and still imprecise about the exact figure a deadline depends on.

questions.from: This module — What never to put in: your data, other people's data
questions.prompt: Why does another person's private information in a document call for a stricter redaction standard than your own?

options.label: You can set your own risk tolerance for your own data, but you don't have standing to make that call for someone else's private information
It doesn't — the same standard applies regardless of whose data it is
Other people's data is always less sensitive than your own

questions.explanation: Consenting to a privacy tradeoff for yourself is a decision only you can make for yourself, not one you can make for someone else.

questions.from: Previous module — Explanations at the level you're actually at
questions.prompt: Why doesn't 'explain this simply' reliably produce an explanation at the right level?

options.label: It names a direction, not your actual existing knowledge, so the model has to guess a default level
It always produces an explanation that's too advanced
It only fails for technical topics

questions.explanation: Stating existing knowledge directly gives a real calibration anchor that 'simply' alone doesn't provide.

questions.from: Previous module — Asking it to quiz you rather than tell you
questions.prompt: Why does reading a clear explanation not reliably build the ability to use a concept later?

options.label: Reading tests recognition; using the concept later requires recall, a different and harder skill
Reading and recall are the same cognitive process
It's only true for complex technical topics

questions.explanation: Recognition and generation are genuinely different cognitive tasks.

questions.from: Previous module — The illusion of understanding a good explanation
questions.prompt: What's a genuine sign of understanding rather than just fluency?

options.label: Being able to explain the concept unaided, with no source open
The explanation feeling completely clear while reading it
Finishing the explanation quickly

questions.explanation: Real signs of understanding remove the source; felt clarity while reading measures the explanation, not your retention.

questions.from: Previous module — Learning from an explanation that might be wrong
questions.prompt: Why is a wrong explanation especially costly for a true beginner?

options.label: A beginner has no independent basis to notice the error, so it becomes the foundation later understanding builds on
Beginners are less careful readers than experts
It isn't more costly — expertise doesn't change detection odds

questions.explanation: Noticing an inconsistency requires prior knowledge to compare against, which a beginner doesn't have yet.

questions.from: Older — Drafting, editing and critique are three different asks
questions.prompt: Why is 'make this better,' with a draft pasted in, an ambiguous instruction?

options.label: It names a goal but not a method, leaving the model to guess between editing in place and rewriting from scratch
It's unambiguous — it always means a full rewrite
The ambiguity only affects very short pieces of writing

questions.explanation: Naming the method — draft, edit, or critique — removes the ambiguity 'make this better' leaves open.

questions.from: Older — Summaries that keep the caveats
questions.prompt: Why do AI summaries tend to drop caveats and hedges specifically?

options.label: A hedge makes a sentence longer and less confident-sounding, which summarisation is usually optimizing against
Caveats are usually incorrect, so removing them improves accuracy
Hedges only appear in very long documents

questions.explanation: Caveats are exactly the qualifying, secondary-sounding content a compression process treats as trimmable.
